chapters.summary: Staff welcomes attendees to the joint Committee on Veterans and General Welfare hearing, asks everyone to silence electronic devices, and states that no one should approach the dais.
chapters.title: Council staff opens joint hearing and sets housekeeping rules

utterances.speaker: Council Staff
utterances.text: Good morning and welcome to today's New York City Council hearing from the Committee of Veterans joined with the Committee on General Welfare.

utterances.speaker: Council Staff
utterances.text: At this time, I'd like to remind everyone to please silence their electronic devices and at no point is anyone to approach the dais.

utterances.speaker: Council Staff
utterances.text: Chairs, we're ready to begin.

chapters.summary: Morano welcomes a packed room, expresses excitement for the joint hearing with General Welfare, and says he sought the Veterans chairmanship to help people who often do not get the help they deserve.
chapters.title: Chair Morano opens joint hearing on veteran homelessness

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: Hello, everyone.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: I am Councilmember Frank Morano.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: I have the privilege of being the chair of the Committee on Veterans, and this is my kind of hearing.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: Not only do I love to see a packed house, both at the testimony table and not an available seat to be had in the crowd, which hopefully means we'll have a lot of members of the public testifying.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: I'm also hoping we'll have a lot of folks testifying on Zoom.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: But when I sought to have this chairmanship, I really sought to do it because I thought this would be a position where I could really help a lot of people,

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: particularly people who don't get the help that they deserve from the city, the state, and the federal government, in spite of the fact that they're still the first to help others.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: So I'm excited about this, and I'm particularly excited that it is a joint committee hearing with the Committee on General Welfare.

chapters.summary: Morano introduces Chair Hudson, notes their political differences but shared commitment to veteran homelessness, cites 140,000-150,000 New Yorkers needing help, and reports homeless veterans dropped from 1,558 in 2015 to 697 in 2025 but rose from 482 in 2022.
chapters.title: Morano highlights bipartisan partnership and veteran homelessness data

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: I'm joined by my colleague, Councilmember Crystal Hudson, Chair of the Committee on General Welfare.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: And we're doing this joint oversight hearing on one of the most important issues facing New York today, and that's the issue of veteran homelessness in New York City.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: Thank you for joining us to discuss this important topic.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: I was so eager to co-chair this hearing with Councilmember Hudson, not only because of my respect for her as a councilmember, but because we do not see the world the same way.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: We come from different political parties, different ideologies, different boroughs, different genders.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: If there's a difference chart, we're just about on a different page when it comes to everything.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: But we're on the same page when it comes to the importance of needing to do something about veteran homelessness.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: And in addition to hopefully getting a lot of great ideas in terms of future legislation, in addition to shining a light on some things that need to be shining a light on, in addition to enhancing our own edification of some real issues that veterans are facing

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: and at the conditions at Borden Avenue specifically, my hope is that by having two people like us who come from totally different corners of the world

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: addressing this problem in a very real way and take it seriously, hopefully this is a wake-up call to the

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: 8.5 million New Yorkers that might not be attuned to this issue, that we have 140,000 to 150,000 people that could really use help in this city.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: And that's why I'm excited about this.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: Many communities across the country, New York City continues to face a homelessness crisis driven by rising housing costs and a shortage of affordable housing, among other things.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: And our veterans are not immune to these challenges.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: And ensuring that those who served our country have access to stable housing remains a critical responsibility.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: Now, the good news is New York City has made significant progress in reducing veteran homelessness over the past decade.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: In 2025, there were 697 homeless veterans in New York City.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: That's down from 1,558 homeless veterans in 2015.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: That's a 44% decrease.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: I can promise you I'm going to be working pretty hard on this issue until that number goes from 697 to zero.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: There's no excuse for veteran homelessness in New York City as far as I'm concerned.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: And the successes that we've had are due in part to the coordinated efforts of DVS, DSS, and their partners.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: We're going to hear from them all today.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: Veterans experiencing homelessness can access emergency shelter, transitional housing, rental assistance, case management, and permanent housing opportunities.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: And these services have helped many veterans move from homelessness to permanent housing and achieve long-term stability.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: However, between 2015 and 2020,

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: Between 2022 and 2025, the number of homeless veterans has increased a little bit.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: Since 2022, we have seen an increase from 482 to 297 individuals.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: So while we're in a much better position from where we were 10 years ago, we're not in as good of a position as where we were four years ago.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: What's going on?

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: What's driving that?

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: Why do we have more homeless veterans now than we did in 2022?

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: And more importantly, what can we do about it?

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: So this increase is raising a lot of important questions about whether existing housing resources, supportive services, and homelessness prevention efforts are keeping pace with current needs.

chapters.summary: Morano discusses conditions at Borden Avenue, uncertainty over VA grant and per diem funding, the city's decision to opt out, and the need to avoid disruptions; he then lists Intro 1051, Intro 0897, Res 0560, and Res 0634.
chapters.title: Morano focuses on Borden Avenue, federal funding, and legislation

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: Specifically, we are going to be diving headfirst into what's going on over at the Borden Avenue Veterans Shelter.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: Councilmember Hudson has been there.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: I've been there.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: Councilmember Wong has been there.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: I know a number of members of the committee and a number of council members who are not on my committee have been there, and we all have independent observations, and we're going to be

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: posing the questions about what we observed to all the folks that you're going to hear from today.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: There's also a whole lot of uncertainty surrounding federal funding for the Borden Avenue Veterans residents, and there are conflicting explanations that have been offered regarding the facility's exclusion from the latest VA.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: grant and per diem funding awards.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: What's going on here?

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: Is this something that's easily rectifiable?

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: And beyond what's going on here, can we make sure that every veteran that had

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: a bed that was paid for by this VA grant sees no disruption in that bed because of the city's decision to opt out of this grant?

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: So the city has committed to maintaining services.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: Questions remain about how lost federal funding is going to be replaced and what impact, if any, the funding dispute may have on operations.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: The discussion has also renewed attention to reported concerns about the conditions at the shelter and the quality of life for veterans living there.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: At the time when veterans'homelessness is rising, it's pretty important that there are absolutely no disruptions, not just to housing, but to the supportive services that veterans are seeking there.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: And it's equally important that efforts to move veterans from shelter into permanent housing remain a priority regardless of the recent events affecting funding.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: And today's hearing is an opportunity to examine the effectiveness of the city's response, identifying remaining gaps, and ensure that veterans experiencing homelessness

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: receive the necessary support they need to secure and maintain permanent housing.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: In addition to our oversight topic today, we will be hearing about a number of pieces of legislation.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: Intro number 1050.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: sponsored by me, which would amend the administrative code in relation to alternative exemption for seriously disabled veterans.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: I'll talk more about that in a minute, and hopefully we'll hear some testimony from DVS and from the public about this.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: We're going to be hearing introduction number 0897, sponsored by Councilmember Felice, which would amend the administrative code in relation to the Department of Social Services'response to certain severe winter weather conditions.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: We're going to be hearing resolution number 0560, sponsored by Councilmember Palladino, which is calling on the federal government to enact the Fair Access to Co-ops for Veterans Act.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: And we're going to be hearing resolution number 0634, which I've also sponsored, which is seeking to recognize 501C19 veteran organizations and designate the week that includes November 11th

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: annually as Veterans Organizations Awareness Week.

chapters.summary: Morano acknowledges Hudson's partnership on the oversight hearing and thanks legislative counsel, analysts, and staff for preparing, then turns the floor to Hudson.
chapters.title: Morano thanks Hudson and committee staff

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: Before I conclude, I want to acknowledge Councilmember Hudson, chair of the Committee on General Welfare, for working with me on this oversight hearing.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: And it's clear that she recognizes as much as I do how crucial it is to address the housing issues veterans face and the barriers to safe and stable shelter that a lot of people still experience.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: I'd also like to thank the committee staff, Legislative Counsel Hannah Cohn, Legislative Analyst Raina Lee, Legislative Policy Analyst.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: Mahnoor Boot, Justin Campos, and Nina Rosenberg, Senior Financial Analyst Sandra Gray, and Community Liaison Sebastian Neme for their hard work in preparing for this hearing.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: I'd also like to thank my staff for their work as we continue to serve our constituents and the city as a whole.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: I'm looking forward to today's testimony and to strengthening support for veterans experiencing homelessness in New York City.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: I'll now turn things over to Chair Hudson to give her opening statement.

chapters.summary: Hudson jokes with Morano about their similarities and differences, welcomes veterans, families, caregivers, service providers, and advocates to the hearing.
chapters.title: Chair Hudson opens with light banter and welcome

utterances.speaker: Crystal Hudson
utterances.text: Thank you so much, Chair Marano.

utterances.speaker: Crystal Hudson
utterances.text: And you know, you went through a litany of differences that we have, but a couple of similarities.

utterances.speaker: Crystal Hudson
utterances.text: I will say one, we're both parents.

utterances.speaker: Crystal Hudson
utterances.text: And your siblings live in my district, so you've got some pretty smart siblings.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: I don't want to tell you who their favorite council member is.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: Not me.

utterances.speaker: Crystal Hudson
utterances.text: Good morning, everyone.

utterances.speaker: Crystal Hudson
utterances.text: My name is Crystal Hudson.

utterances.speaker: Crystal Hudson
utterances.text: I'm chair of the General Welfare Committee, and my pronouns are she, her.

utterances.speaker: Crystal Hudson
utterances.text: I want to welcome our veterans, their families, caregivers, service providers, and advocates who have joined us today.

utterances.speaker: Crystal Hudson
utterances.text: Your input is invaluable to the work of this committee and plays an important role in what we do moving forward.

chapters.summary: Hudson notes approximately 700 homeless veterans in NYC, calls the number unacceptable, aims to hear from providers and advocates, and recounts her Borden Avenue visit with Commissioner Dalton, saying veterans are not getting what they deserve.
chapters.title: Hudson cites ~700 homeless veterans and Borden visit

utterances.speaker: Crystal Hudson
utterances.text: As of the most recent data released on veteran homelessness in New York City, there are approximately 700 homeless veterans in our city, including those that are living in shelter.

utterances.speaker: Crystal Hudson
utterances.text: While this number represents a decline in the number of homeless veterans since 2014, it is still unacceptable.

utterances.speaker: Crystal Hudson
utterances.text: These are New Yorkers who valiantly served our nation.

utterances.speaker: Crystal Hudson
utterances.text: at an enormous personal cost and who upon returning home are counting on their city to guide them into stable and permanent housing.

utterances.speaker: Crystal Hudson
utterances.text: Our aim with this hearing is to hear from the city's providers, veterans, and homeless advocates about how we can improve the services we provide to our veterans.

utterances.speaker: Crystal Hudson
utterances.text: The hope is to have a productive, cordial discussion.

utterances.speaker: Crystal Hudson
utterances.text: Where we learn more about what is happening on the ground, what the council can do as an oversight and legislative body, and how we ultimately get our veterans housed.

utterances.speaker: Crystal Hudson
utterances.text: I'd like to mention and thank Commissioner Dalton for joining me last night in our visit to the Borden Avenue Veterans Shelter.

utterances.speaker: Crystal Hudson
utterances.text: I think the commissioner has done a lot of work to address the specific shelter and the issues there.

utterances.speaker: Crystal Hudson
utterances.text: We spoke with a number of veterans at the shelter last night, and I think ultimately what we can all agree on is that they are not getting what they should as veterans.

utterances.speaker: Crystal Hudson
utterances.text: And that's not even in terms of the specifics at the shelter, but broadly, culturally, I will say in this country, I don't think we're providing veterans with all that they need and that they rightly deserve.

chapters.summary: Hudson thanks the administration, Morano, colleagues, advocates, veteran service organizations, and committee staff, then returns the mic to Morano.
chapters.title: Hudson thanks administration, colleagues, and staff

utterances.speaker: Crystal Hudson
utterances.text: I'd like to thank the administration for being here, Chair Marano, and my colleagues for their constructive engagement and advocates, veteran service organizations, and families for joining us.

utterances.speaker: Crystal Hudson
utterances.text: I also want to thank committee staff for their work on this hearing.

utterances.speaker: Crystal Hudson
utterances.text: The names have already been mentioned, but I'll say them again.

utterances.speaker: Crystal Hudson
utterances.text: Hannah Cohn, Penina Rosenberg, and Justin K.

utterances.speaker: Crystal Hudson
utterances.text: And I'd also like to thank my staff, Andrew Wright, Elika Ruentan, Demi Brown, and Maddie Moorhead.

utterances.speaker: Crystal Hudson
utterances.text: And with that, I'll return the mic back to Chair Marano.

utterances.speaker: Crystal Hudson
utterances.text: Thank you.

chapters.summary: Morano thanks Peter Spencer, acknowledges Councilmembers Wong, De La Rosa, and Paladino, and praises Paladino's advocacy for joint hearings on veteran issues.
chapters.title: Morano acknowledges Republican Conference director and colleagues

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: Thank you, Chair Hudson.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: I also was negligent in not acknowledging and thanking the man who's got the toughest job in city government, the executive director of the New York City Republican Conference, Peter Spencer, who's been

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: a big help, not just in this hearing, but in everything that we do.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: I want to acknowledge several of my colleagues on the Veterans Committee that are here,

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: Councilmember Wong, Councilmember De La Rosa, who people are still talking about from the incredible job that she did chairing these AI hearings,

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: and Councilmember Vicki Palladino, who I have to tell you, in addition to representing more veterans in her district than all of the rest of us,

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: she has really been the most vocal about the need for this committee

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: to pursue joint hearings with other committees because of all the common areas that veteran issues go along with throughout the rest of the city.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: And I have to tell you, this hearing is largely a byproduct of her energy and her insistence that we do that.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: And I have to tell you, so far, all of these joint hearings I've found to be incredibly informative and incredibly productive.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: So, Councilmember Paldino, thank you for your advocacy for veterans.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: And before we begin, I would love for you to speak.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: about your resolution, which I'm proud to sponsor.

chapters.summary: Paladino explains Res 0560 to allow veterans to use VA home loan benefits for co-ops, cites Grace Meng's federal bill and her parents' WWII loan, then calls Borden Avenue a disgrace and notes the city budget provides only $6.5 million for veterans.
chapters.title: Paladino presents co-op resolution and criticizes Borden conditions

utterances.speaker: Vickie Paladino
utterances.text: Thank you, Frank, and thank you to everybody who came out this morning.

utterances.speaker: Vickie Paladino
utterances.text: You know, the main argument is simple.

utterances.speaker: Vickie Paladino
utterances.text: Veterans served our country and should have the opportunity to use their VA home loan benefits to purchase a co-op or a condo, just as they use their benefits to purchase home loans.

utterances.speaker: Vickie Paladino
utterances.text: That's how my mother and father got their home.

utterances.speaker: Vickie Paladino
utterances.text: My father was a World War II vet.

utterances.speaker: Vickie Paladino
utterances.text: And they got their loan through the veterans.

utterances.speaker: Vickie Paladino
utterances.text: I'd like to see the expansion of home ownership opportunities, allowing eligible veterans, service members, and surviving spouses to use the VA-backed loans to purchase their co-ops.

utterances.speaker: Vickie Paladino
utterances.text: We need to address New York City's housing markets.

utterances.speaker: Vickie Paladino
utterances.text: Co-ops and condos make up a significant portion of New York City's housing market and can offer a more affordable alternative to any other types of homes.

utterances.speaker: Vickie Paladino
utterances.text: Helping the veterans to build equality and equity.

utterances.speaker: Vickie Paladino
utterances.text: Make it easier for eligible veterans to purchase a home, build financial stability, and put down roots in their communities.

utterances.speaker: Vickie Paladino
utterances.text: The bottom line here is veterans should not face unnecessary barriers to home ownership simply because they live.

utterances.speaker: Vickie Paladino
utterances.text: in a city where co-ops are common.

utterances.speaker: Vickie Paladino
utterances.text: This resolution calls on Congress and the President of the United States to advance legislation that expands access to home ownership

utterances.speaker: Vickie Paladino
utterances.text: and gives eligible veterans more housing options, particularly in New York City.

utterances.speaker: Vickie Paladino
utterances.text: So we call upon, you know, Grace Meng introduced a great bill down in Washington.

utterances.speaker: Vickie Paladino
utterances.text: I have a terrific relationship with Congressman Meng.

utterances.speaker: Vickie Paladino
utterances.text: And I'd like to see this sped up through her work with me together at the state level.

utterances.speaker: Vickie Paladino
utterances.text: So that's basically all I have to say about that.

utterances.speaker: Vickie Paladino
utterances.text: Our veterans are not treated fairly.

utterances.speaker: Vickie Paladino
utterances.text: We know that.

utterances.speaker: Vickie Paladino
utterances.text: We visited Borden Avenue, and I have to say we're being very kind in our description of Borden Avenue.

utterances.speaker: Vickie Paladino
utterances.text: Borden Avenue is an absolute disgrace.

utterances.speaker: Vickie Paladino
utterances.text: And the idea that we only have the one homeless shelter here in Queens, known as Borden Avenue, and it's in the condition that it's in, is shameful.

utterances.speaker: Vickie Paladino
utterances.text: And we should be ashamed of ourselves.

utterances.speaker: Vickie Paladino
utterances.text: We passed a $126 million budget.

utterances.speaker: Vickie Paladino
utterances.text: You hear me say this at almost every committee hearing I talk at.

utterances.speaker: Vickie Paladino
utterances.text: We passed a $126 billion budget, and out of that budget, only $6.5 million goes to our veterans.

utterances.speaker: Vickie Paladino
utterances.text: So as a committee, we have a lot of work to do.

utterances.speaker: Vickie Paladino
utterances.text: And the first thing we need to do is stir up some real money, whether it comes from private entities, but we need to reinvent.

utterances.speaker: Vickie Paladino
utterances.text: how the veterans are going to be, how we could finance the veterans.

utterances.speaker: Vickie Paladino
utterances.text: Because obviously the city is falling behind.

utterances.speaker: Vickie Paladino
utterances.text: We're going to get to a lot of that work today.

utterances.speaker: Vickie Paladino
utterances.text: Okay, thank you, everybody.

chapters.summary: Morano thanks Paladino, acknowledges Councilmembers Wilson, Nurse, Aviles, and Ung, and turns to committee counsel, who administers the affirmation to the administration witnesses and reminds them to state their names for the record.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.text: As a reminder to all of our witnesses, please state your name prior to testimony for the record.

utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Council Staff

chapters.summary: Mata introduces herself as DVS Commissioner, says housing is fundamental, recognizes shared responsibility for veterans, and describes veteran homelessness as varied, with DVS providing an end-to-end housing approach and maintaining a presence at Borden Avenue.
chapters.title: DVS Commissioner Mata testifies on housing commitment and DVS approach

utterances.speaker: Yesenia Mata
utterances.text: Good morning, Chair Murano, Chair Hudson, and distinguished members of the Committees on Veterans and General Welfare.

utterances.speaker: Yesenia Mata
utterances.text: My name is Yesenia Mata, and I have the honor of serving as Commissioner of the New York City Department of Veteran Services.

utterances.speaker: Yesenia Mata
utterances.text: Thank you for the opportunity to testify today on the critical issue of veteran

utterances.speaker: Yesenia Mata
utterances.text: homelessness and to highlight the work our agency is doing to ensure that veterans and their families have access to safe, stable, and permanent housing.

utterances.speaker: Yesenia Mata
utterances.text: I also want to take a moment to recognize the many individuals who, while they may not have served in uniform themselves, continue to stand alongside our veterans in service to them.

utterances.speaker: Yesenia Mata
utterances.text: From our city council members, government partners, and nonprofit organizations, to housing providers, advocates, and community members,

utterances.speaker: Yesenia Mata
utterances.text: their commitment reminds us that supporting those who have served is not solely the responsibility of veterans or any one agency.

utterances.speaker: Yesenia Mata
utterances.text: It is a shared responsibility that requires all of us working together.

utterances.speaker: Yesenia Mata
utterances.text: As a soldier and a military spouse, I understand that service does not end when someone takes off the uniform.

utterances.speaker: Yesenia Mata
utterances.text: Neither should our commitment to the people who have served.

utterances.speaker: Yesenia Mata
utterances.text: Every veteran deserves the opportunity to live with dignity, stability, and a sense of

utterances.speaker: Yesenia Mata
utterances.text: belonging in the city they call home.

utterances.speaker: Yesenia Mata
utterances.text: Housing is fundamental to that commitment.

utterances.speaker: Yesenia Mata
utterances.text: When we talk about veteran homelessness, we are not talking about a single experience or a single pathway into crisis.

utterances.speaker: Yesenia Mata
utterances.text: Some veterans are staying in shelter, others are facing eviction, struggling to pay rent, or living in unstable situations that may not immediately be visible.

utterances.speaker: Yesenia Mata
utterances.text: Some are navigating physical or mental health challenges, disability, employment transitions, or complicated benefit systems.

utterances.speaker: Yesenia Mata
utterances.text: Our responsibility is to see the whole person and intervene as early as possible.

utterances.speaker: Yesenia Mata
utterances.text: That is the purpose of our Housing and Supported Services team.

utterances.speaker: Yesenia Mata
utterances.text: DVS provides an end-to-end veteran-centered approach that begins with outreach, intake, and assessment,

utterances.speaker: Yesenia Mata
utterances.text: continues through housing navigation, applications, subsidy coordination, inspections, and lease follow-up, and extends into aftercare and housing retention.

utterances.speaker: Yesenia Mata
utterances.text: Our work is grounding...

utterances.speaker: Yesenia Mata
utterances.text: Grounded in a housing first oriented trauma informed approach, recognizing that permanent housing is a foundation from which other aspects of stability can grow.

utterances.speaker: Yesenia Mata
utterances.text: Veterans come to DVS through community partners, shelter providers, VA facilities, direct outreach, walkings, and referrals.

utterances.speaker: Yesenia Mata
utterances.text: It is important to our agency to meet veterans where they are at.

utterances.speaker: Yesenia Mata
utterances.text: For example, although the Borden Avenue veteran

utterances.speaker: Yesenia Mata
utterances.text: Veterans resident is not designated as a veteran resource center under the New York City Charter, DVS maintains a presence to provide resources and services to residents.

utterances.speaker: Yesenia Mata
utterances.text: No matter where a veteran may be, our staff works with each individual to understand their housing status, income, benefits, safety concerns, and immediate needs.

utterances.speaker: Yesenia Mata
utterances.text: Together, they develop an individualized housing plan.

utterances.speaker: Yesenia Mata
utterances.text: That plan may involve locating an apartment, arranging a viewing, gathering documentation, coordinating with a landlord, or identifying the subsidy best suited to the veteran's circumstances.

chapters.summary: Mata describes vouchers including HUD-VASH, CityFHEPS, and Section 8, DVS's role navigating agencies, placements growing from 55 in FY22 to 209 in FY26, aftercare contacts through 22 months, and prevention coordination with partner agencies.
chapters.title: Mata details housing pathways, placements, and prevention coordination

utterances.speaker: Yesenia Mata
utterances.text: No single voucher or housing program meets every need.

utterances.speaker: Yesenia Mata
utterances.text: DVS helps veterans navigate pathways that include the Veteran Focus CCM voucher, CityFABS Section 8 administered through NYSHA or HPD, and HUD-VASH in partnership with the United States Department of Veteran Affairs.

utterances.speaker: Yesenia Mata
utterances.text: We also assist with documentation for one-shot deals when emergency financial assistance can help address arrears or other housing costs.

utterances.speaker: Yesenia Mata
utterances.text: Importantly, DVS does not independently control eligibility determination, inspection, payment, or approval.

utterances.speaker: Yesenia Mata
utterances.text: Our role is to help the veteran navigate those steps and keep the process moving across agencies.

utterances.speaker: Yesenia Mata
utterances.text: We have seen meaningful progress.

utterances.speaker: Yesenia Mata
utterances.text: According to our July 2026 VetStat reporting, DVS permanent housing placements grew from 55

utterances.speaker: Yesenia Mata
utterances.text: in FY22 to 119 in FY23, 126 in FY24, 153 in FY25, and 209 in FY26.

utterances.speaker: Yesenia Mata
utterances.text: In FY26, our team also completed 318 housing viewings and assisted with 231 affordable housing applications.

utterances.speaker: Yesenia Mata
utterances.text: These numbers represent individual veterans taking steps toward greater stability and the sustained work staff and partners behind each placement.

utterances.speaker: Yesenia Mata
utterances.text: But a placement is not the end of our responsibility.

utterances.speaker: Yesenia Mata
utterances.text: I want to emphasize this point.

utterances.speaker: Yesenia Mata
utterances.text: Giving a veteran the keys to an apartment is a major milestone, but helping that veteran keep those keys is just as important.

utterances.speaker: Yesenia Mata
utterances.text: A veteran may still need help with benefits, recertification, employment, food, health care, or unexpected financial emergency.

utterances.speaker: Yesenia Mata
utterances.text: Without that continued support, a housing placement can remain fragile.

utterances.speaker: Yesenia Mata
utterances.text: Our current aftercare framework includes scheduled follow-up contacts extending through 22 months after placement.

utterances.speaker: Yesenia Mata
utterances.text: Those contacts help staff identify rent or subsidy issues, housing conditions, safety concerns, and other threats to stability.

utterances.speaker: Yesenia Mata
utterances.text: In FY26, 702 veterans answered an aftercare call, according to our July reporting.

utterances.speaker: Yesenia Mata
utterances.text: We are also examining ways to strengthen it.

utterances.speaker: Yesenia Mata
utterances.text: early follow-up, and more consistently connect veterans to the broader supports they need.

utterances.speaker: Yesenia Mata
utterances.text: Any proposed enhancements remain subject to review and approval.

utterances.speaker: Yesenia Mata
utterances.text: Our existing policy remains in effect.

utterances.speaker: Yesenia Mata
utterances.text: Prevention must be part of the same conversation.

utterances.speaker: Yesenia Mata
utterances.text: When we identify a veteran at risk of losing housing, we can coordinate referrals for financial assistance, legal support, landlord engagement, benefits, and other services before the instability becomes homelessness.

utterances.speaker: Yesenia Mata
utterances.text: A successful housing system should be measured not only by how many people move into permanent housing, but also by how many remain there.

utterances.speaker: Yesenia Mata
utterances.text: None of this work happens in isolation.

utterances.speaker: Yesenia Mata
utterances.text: We rely on close coordination with the Department of Homeless Services, DSS, NHRA, NYSHA, HPD, and the VA, shelter

utterances.speaker: Yesenia Mata
utterances.text: operators, property owners, nonprofit housing providers, and legal and community-based organizations.

utterances.speaker: Yesenia Mata
utterances.text: Each partner has a distinct role.

utterances.speaker: Yesenia Mata
utterances.text: DVS helps bring those roles together around the veteran and their housing plan.

utterances.speaker: Yesenia Mata
utterances.text: That coordination is particularly important when a case requires multiple documents, inspections, agency approvals, and payments processed before a move can take place.

utterances.speaker: Yesenia Mata
utterances.text: We also recognize that housing needs intersect with mental health, employment, and family stability.

utterances.speaker: Yesenia Mata
utterances.text: A veteran seeking an apartment may need a connection to health care.

utterances.speaker: Yesenia Mata
utterances.text: A veteran who has moved in may need help securing employment or accessing benefits.

utterances.speaker: Yesenia Mata
utterances.text: Our team works with veterans serving and community partners to make those connections rather than treating housing as a standalone transaction.

chapters.summary: Mata says DVS will emphasize faster housing pathways, landlord relationships, eviction prevention, aftercare, and equitable access for women, LGBTQ+, older, and disabled veterans; she concludes by supporting the intent of Intro 1051 and deferring to the Department of Finance.
chapters.title: Mata outlines strategic direction and supports Intro 1051

utterances.speaker: Yesenia Mata
utterances.text: Looking ahead, our strategic direction emphasizes faster pathways to permanent housing, stronger landlord relationship, earlier eviction prevention, comprehensive aftercare, and better performance tracking.

utterances.speaker: Yesenia Mata
utterances.text: We also want to strengthen equitable access for women veterans, LGBTQ plus veterans, older veterans, veterans with disabilities, and communities that may face additional barrier to services.

utterances.speaker: Yesenia Mata
utterances.text: We must continue improving how we measure placement timelines, voucher utilization, and long-term housing retention so that we understand where the system works and where it needs attention.

utterances.speaker: Yesenia Mata
utterances.text: I want to be clear, our work is not complete when a veteran exits shelter, and it is not complete when a housing application is approved.

utterances.speaker: Yesenia Mata
utterances.text: It is complete only when we have done everything within our role to help that veteran build lasting stability.

utterances.speaker: Yesenia Mata
utterances.text: That requires coordination, accountability, and a willingness to keep improving our systems.

utterances.speaker: Yesenia Mata
utterances.text: Our veterans have served this country in different eras, in different capacities, and with different experiences.

utterances.speaker: Yesenia Mata
utterances.text: They deserve a city that recognizes their service, not only through ceremonies and words of appreciation,

utterances.speaker: Yesenia Mata
utterances.text: but through a practical pathway to save stable housing and the support needed to remain there.

utterances.speaker: Yesenia Mata
utterances.text: Lastly, on Intro 1051, the Department of Veterans Services supports the intent of this bill and defers to our colleagues at the NYC Department of Finance.

utterances.speaker: Yesenia Mata
utterances.text: Thank you for the opportunity to testify and for the Council's continued attention to the needs of New York City's veterans and military-connected community.

utterances.speaker: Yesenia Mata
utterances.text: I look forward to our continued partnership and happy to answer any questions.

chapters.summary: Dalton introduces herself as DSS Commissioner, introduces Deputy Commissioner Sonia Russell, notes over 200,000 veterans in NYC, and says the city has one of the lowest veteran homeless rates in the country.
chapters.title: DSS Commissioner Dalton begins testimony on veteran homelessness

utterances.speaker: Erin Dalton
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: Erin Dalton
utterances.text: Good morning, Chair Hudson, Chair Marano, members of the Committee on General Welfare, and members of the Committee on Veterans.

utterances.speaker: Erin Dalton
utterances.text: I am Erin Dalton, and I serve as the Commissioner of the Department of Social Services.

utterances.speaker: Erin Dalton
utterances.text: Joining me today is Deputy Commissioner for Adult Services Shelter Operations, Sonia Russell.

utterances.speaker: Erin Dalton
utterances.text: Thank you for convening today's oversight hearing on veterans'homelessness in New York City.

utterances.speaker: Erin Dalton
utterances.text: The New York City Department of Veteran Services, or DVS, estimates that there are more than 200,000 veterans who call New York City home.

utterances.speaker: Erin Dalton
utterances.text: We thank them and all U.S.

utterances.speaker: Erin Dalton
utterances.text: Veterans for their service.

utterances.speaker: Erin Dalton
utterances.text: New York City has demonstrated its commitment to veterans experiencing homelessness.

utterances.speaker: Erin Dalton
utterances.text: We opened the first veteran-specific shelter in the country, led the country in efforts to get to functional zero in veterans'homelessness, and today have one of the lowest veteran homeless rates of anywhere in the country.

utterances.speaker: Erin Dalton
utterances.text: In the 2026 point in time count, we counted 791 veterans in shelter and only one on shelter.

utterances.speaker: Erin Dalton
utterances.text: person who identified as a veteran.

chapters.summary: Dalton describes how DHS identifies veterans at intake, verifies status, places single men at BAVR, offers women veterans two ICL shelters with set-aside beds, and prioritizes families with children near schools.
chapters.title: Dalton explains DHS veteran identification and shelter placement

utterances.speaker: Erin Dalton
utterances.text: I would like to start with an explanation of how we identify and serve veterans in the DHS homelessness system.

utterances.speaker: Erin Dalton
utterances.text: Every person who comes to DHS intake is asked whether they served in the U.S.

utterances.speaker: Erin Dalton
utterances.text: Military.

utterances.speaker: Erin Dalton
utterances.text: When someone identifies as a veteran, DHS conducts a verification utilizing the

utterances.speaker: Erin Dalton
utterances.text: Veterans Affairs Square system.

utterances.speaker: Erin Dalton
utterances.text: When a veteran is placed, where a veteran is placed depends on whether they identify as a single adult man, a single adult woman, part of an adult family, or part of a family with children.

utterances.speaker: Erin Dalton
utterances.text: For single adult men who report as self-reported veteran status, they are offered a bed at Board and Area Veterans Residence, BAVR.

utterances.speaker: Erin Dalton
utterances.text: If BAVR has no bed available or if they prefer a different setting, they are offered another DHS shelter.

utterances.speaker: Erin Dalton
utterances.text: At BAVR, the site's operator, the Institute for Community Living, or ICL, completes intake, including screenings for physical health, mental health, substance use, and disability needs.

utterances.speaker: Erin Dalton
utterances.text: Until October 1 of this year, ICL ran two programs in the same building at BAVR.

utterances.speaker: Erin Dalton
utterances.text: A VA-funded program that's partly funded and overseen by the U.S.

utterances.speaker: Erin Dalton
utterances.text: Department of Veterans Affairs through its Grant and Per Diem, or GPD, program, and a DHS veterans program funded and overseen by DHS for everyone else at the site.

utterances.speaker: Erin Dalton
utterances.text: Every veteran DHS referred to BAVR was assessed for the GPD program.

utterances.speaker: Erin Dalton
utterances.text: The VA decided eligibility using its own criteria, including military discharge status, eligibility,

utterances.speaker: Erin Dalton
utterances.text: for VA health care and willingness to follow program rules.

utterances.speaker: Erin Dalton
utterances.text: Veterans the VA accepted joined the GPD program.

utterances.speaker: Erin Dalton
utterances.text: Veterans the VA found ineligible or who chose not to take part were placed in the DHS program.

chapters.summary: Dalton says the VA-funded GPD program at BAVR ended, there is no longer separate VA eligibility, and DVS, VA, and SSVF continue on site while DHS's Veterans Service Unit connects veterans to services.
chapters.title: Dalton says GPD program at BAVR ended, all veterans now in DHS program

utterances.speaker: Erin Dalton
utterances.text: The GPD program at BAVR has now ended.

utterances.speaker: Erin Dalton
utterances.text: There's no longer a separate VA eligibility decision and every veteran at BAVR is placed in the DHS program.

utterances.speaker: Erin Dalton
utterances.text: DHS program.

utterances.speaker: Erin Dalton
utterances.text: Staff from the New York City Department of Veteran Services, the VA, and the Supportive Services for Veteran Families, or SSVF, continue to work on site.

utterances.speaker: Erin Dalton
utterances.text: For single adult women, women veterans are offered placement at one of two ICL-run shelters with beds set aside for veterans.

utterances.speaker: Erin Dalton
utterances.text: DHS does not have a separate shelter only for women veterans.

utterances.speaker: Erin Dalton
utterances.text: As of October 18th, 55 women in our DHS shelter program identified as veterans.

utterances.speaker: Erin Dalton
utterances.text: For adult families, the process is similar.

utterances.speaker: Erin Dalton
utterances.text: Any member of the family who self-reports as a veteran are offered placement at one of two sites with beds set aside for veterans, depending on the family's needs.

utterances.speaker: Erin Dalton
utterances.text: Families with children under 18 apply for shelter at PATH, that's the Prevention Assistance and Temporary Housing Intake Center.

utterances.speaker: Erin Dalton
utterances.text: For families with children who include a veteran, we prioritize as close as possible to the youngest child's school.

utterances.speaker: Erin Dalton
utterances.text: SSVF providers work at PATH to connect these families to SSVF services.

utterances.speaker: Erin Dalton
utterances.text: For all veterans we serve, whenever a veteran is placed in shelter, whether single adult men, single adult women, adult families, or families with children, our shelters work to connect them with appropriate, supportive, and wraparound services.

utterances.speaker: Erin Dalton
utterances.text: Our DHS Veterans Service Unit at DHS partners with DVS and other stakeholders, including SSVF, the VA, and others, to connect veterans to the wealth of local, state, federal, and veteran-specific services in our city,

utterances.speaker: Erin Dalton
utterances.text: including housing services, medical and behavioral health care, city, state, and federal entitlements like public assistance and pension benefits.

utterances.speaker: Erin Dalton
utterances.text: DHS staff lead this work through regular meetings, weekly, biweekly, and monthly, with all stakeholders to stay connected and ensure we are working collaboratively to serve our veterans.

chapters.summary: Dalton says the GPD grant was reduced 70% from 154 beds and $4 million to 44 beds and $1.3 million, included terms conflicting with city and state anti-discrimination laws, so DHS declined and is using city tax levy funds to cover the gap.
chapters.title: Dalton explains federal GPD grant reduction and city's decision to decline

utterances.speaker: Erin Dalton
utterances.text: The Federal Grant and Per Diem Program.

utterances.speaker: Erin Dalton
utterances.text: I would like to explain the funding New York City received from the Federal Grant and Per Diem Program, or GPD.

utterances.speaker: Erin Dalton
utterances.text: The GPD program provides funding to state, local, and community-based partners who provide services to veterans experiencing homelessness, focusing on transitional supportive housing as a stepstone towards permanent housing.

utterances.speaker: Erin Dalton
utterances.text: The VA determines eligibility for these services and placements through the GPD program subsequent to a standard DHS intake process previously described.

utterances.speaker: Erin Dalton
utterances.text: New York City has been a proud recipient of funding from the GPD program for over 15 years leading into 2026.

utterances.speaker: Erin Dalton
utterances.text: With our last three-year funding agreement ending, the Department of Homeless Services applied for a new grant in February 2026.

utterances.speaker: Erin Dalton
utterances.text: In June 2026, the VA responded with their proposed funding for the new grant, and if we had accepted the grant, we would have received an official award letter from the VA in September.

utterances.speaker: Erin Dalton
utterances.text: The grant award, which previously covered 154 beds and up to $4 million, was reduced by 70% to cover only 44 beds and provide up to $1.3 million in funding.

utterances.speaker: Erin Dalton
utterances.text: In addition, for the first time and as a direct result of the federal executive order 14168 defending women gender ideology extremism and restoring biological truth to the federal government

utterances.speaker: Erin Dalton
utterances.text: issued January 20th, 2025, the grant agreement language included terms and conditions that DHS could not agree to.

utterances.speaker: Erin Dalton
utterances.text: For DHS to agree with.

utterances.speaker: Erin Dalton
utterances.text: and comply with the grant's terms and conditions, we would be in violation of state and local laws that protect people from discrimination on the basis of gender.

utterances.speaker: Erin Dalton
utterances.text: Those laws include New York State Law, NYS Executive Law 296-2-A, New York State Regulation 9,

utterances.speaker: Erin Dalton
utterances.text: New York City RR 466.13 and New York City Local Law Administrative Code Title VIII Chapter 8.

utterances.speaker: Erin Dalton
utterances.text: In addition to these legal barriers, the grant's terms and conditions would have required that DHS change the way it operates and introduce discrimination into the intake process, e.g., for example, requiring that we ask questions about biological sex to all people identifying as a veteran.

utterances.speaker: Erin Dalton
utterances.text: Given this, DHS identified city tax levy dollars needed to fill the gap in federal funds and inform the VA that the grant offer was to be declined.

utterances.speaker: Erin Dalton
utterances.text: To reiterate, the agency is now filling this gap with city tax levy funding so no beds or services are lost and every veteran who needs a bed gets one.

utterances.speaker: Erin Dalton
utterances.text: Today, we are serving more veterans at BAVR than we did with the federal funding due to the VA declining many veteran applicants for the grant program.

utterances.speaker: Erin Dalton
utterances.text: When the grant ended on September 30, 2026, 105 individuals were residing at BAVR, which has a capacity of 231.

utterances.speaker: Erin Dalton
utterances.text: As of October 19th, there are 168 individuals residing at BAVR.

utterances.speaker: Erin Dalton
utterances.text: Is now working to fill all available beds at BAVR with veterans from other shelters and new veterans who come into intake.

chapters.summary: Dalton says ICL has run BAVR since 2008, 173 veterans were housed in FY25 and 141 in FY26, serious incidents dropped 44%, 911 calls dropped 48%, and complaints and transfer requests also declined.
chapters.title: Dalton reports BAVR operations and declining incidents

utterances.speaker: Erin Dalton
utterances.text: And a turn to shelter operations and conditions at Borden Avenue Veterans Residence.

utterances.speaker: Erin Dalton
utterances.text: ICL serves as the provider at BAVR.

utterances.speaker: Erin Dalton
utterances.text: ICL has been a provider there since 2008 with the core mission of helping New York City's homeless veteran community improve their physical mental health through wraparound social services, recreational programs to help clients get back on their feet.

utterances.speaker: Erin Dalton
utterances.text: ICL works hard to help their veteran clients transition to permanent homes.

utterances.speaker: Erin Dalton
utterances.text: 173 veterans moved out into housing in FY25, surpassing the annual target of 155, and another 141 veterans moved out into housing in FY26.

utterances.speaker: Erin Dalton
utterances.text: Since January 2026, 55% of clients have gained or maintained employment.

utterances.speaker: Erin Dalton
utterances.text: In addition, all critical measures at Borden are going in the right direction.

utterances.speaker: Erin Dalton
utterances.text: From January 1 to October 1, 2026, the site recorded 377 serious incidents, down 44% from 674 in the same time period in 2025.

utterances.speaker: Erin Dalton
utterances.text: Every major incident category declined, and the most serious types dropped the most.

utterances.speaker: Erin Dalton
utterances.text: Psychiatric emergencies fell by more than half.

utterances.speaker: Erin Dalton
utterances.text: Drug and alcohol incidents fell by 39%.

utterances.speaker: Erin Dalton
utterances.text: Quality of life and failure to comply incidents fell by 35%.

utterances.speaker: Erin Dalton
utterances.text: Fights fell by 31%.

utterances.speaker: Erin Dalton
utterances.text: Calls to 911 show the same improvement.

utterances.speaker: Erin Dalton
utterances.text: From January to September, calls at the site fell 48% from 813.

utterances.speaker: Erin Dalton
utterances.text: Ambulance calls, the largest category, dropped 49%.

utterances.speaker: Erin Dalton
utterances.text: Disputes fell 58%, and reports of theft fell 80%.

utterances.speaker: Erin Dalton
utterances.text: BAVR residents are also filing fewer complaints.

utterances.speaker: Erin Dalton
utterances.text: There were 35 complaints in 2026 compared with 43 in the same time period in 2025.

utterances.speaker: Erin Dalton
utterances.text: Transfer requests from residents asking to leave the site fell by 60% from 10 to 4.

chapters.summary: Dalton says the BAVR Community Advisory Board meets quarterly, house meetings are held twice monthly, and she held a listening session with about 20 veterans who gave positive and negative feedback on conditions, security, and services.
chapters.title: Dalton describes community advisory board and resident listening session

utterances.speaker: Erin Dalton
utterances.text: At DSS, DHS, we work together with ICL to listen to the community around the shelter, as well as veterans staying at the shelter.

utterances.speaker: Erin Dalton
utterances.text: For example, the BAVR Community Advisory Board meets quarterly.

utterances.speaker: Erin Dalton
utterances.text: Three meetings have occurred thus far this year, with a fourth meeting planned for before the end of the year.

utterances.speaker: Erin Dalton
utterances.text: The CAB includes community stakeholders to facilitate open dialogue between providers, DHS, elected officials, community board, and community members.

utterances.speaker: Erin Dalton
utterances.text: CAB meetings offer an opportunity for concerns to be raised, updates about the facility to be shared, successes to be celebrated, and to encourage ongoing constructive collaboration between the shelter and the surrounding community.

utterances.speaker: Erin Dalton
utterances.text: In addition to the cab, ICL has regular house meetings at BAVR.

utterances.speaker: Erin Dalton
utterances.text: House meetings are held twice a month in the afternoon and evening.

utterances.speaker: Erin Dalton
utterances.text: They facilitate open lines of communication between shelter staff and residents.

utterances.speaker: Erin Dalton
utterances.text: Staff have the opportunity to reiterate house rules, share upcoming events, and clients have an opportunity to share their feedback.

utterances.speaker: Erin Dalton
utterances.text: In addition to the quarterly cab, I personally had the opportunity to conduct a listening session with BAVR residents, a company BAVR.

utterances.speaker: Erin Dalton
utterances.text: DHS Administrator Risa Henderson, representatives from the New York City Department of Veteran Services, and ICL leadership.

utterances.speaker: Erin Dalton
utterances.text: During the listening session, we were able to hear from about 20 veterans.

utterances.speaker: Erin Dalton
utterances.text: We received a lot of positive feedback about the site and services and received mixed or negative feedback about building conditions, security, and service provision.

utterances.speaker: Erin Dalton
utterances.text: ICL executive leadership and ICL leadership on site at BAVR have been very receptive to the feedback and a partner in considering implementing improvements at BAVR.

chapters.summary: Dalton outlines a $4.3 million roof and skylight replacement scheduled for 2027-2029, a $2.9 million flood wall, shower privacy partitions to be installed in six to eight weeks, and efforts to improve food and use the commercial kitchen.
chapters.title: Dalton details BAVR repairs: roof, flood wall, showers, food

utterances.speaker: Erin Dalton
utterances.text: DHS is also making a series of repairs and capital improvements at BAVR to fix long-standing problems with the building and protect it for its future.

utterances.speaker: Erin Dalton
utterances.text: Those repairs and improvements include the following.

utterances.speaker: Erin Dalton
utterances.text: The roof and the skylight leaks.

utterances.speaker: Erin Dalton
utterances.text: Until the full roof replacement is complete, DHS is managing leaks in the sleeping area with tarps, which will stay up until further notice.

utterances.speaker: Erin Dalton
utterances.text: Beds in the affected areas will stay offline until the capital work is complete.

utterances.speaker: Erin Dalton
utterances.text: DHS has a contractor on standby to continuously monitor and make temporary repairs to address any leaks that arise from the roof and skylight due to inclement weather.

utterances.speaker: Erin Dalton
utterances.text: Roof and skylight replacement.

utterances.speaker: Erin Dalton
utterances.text: A $4.3 million DHS capital project will replace the building's entire roof and skylights.

utterances.speaker: Erin Dalton
utterances.text: Design is complete and the project will now move to procurement with work scheduled from June 2027 to December 2029.

utterances.speaker: Erin Dalton
utterances.text: Beds under the skylights will stay offline and be taking offline in phases while the skylights are replaced.

utterances.speaker: Erin Dalton
utterances.text: For flood protection.

utterances.speaker: Erin Dalton
utterances.text: A new flood wall will be built behind the building to protect it from future storms.

utterances.speaker: Erin Dalton
utterances.text: Design is complete and the project is scheduled to move to procurement with construction planned for December 2027 through December 2028.

utterances.speaker: Erin Dalton
utterances.text: The project costs $2.9 million.

utterances.speaker: Erin Dalton
utterances.text: Federal resiliency funding secured with the support of Congresswoman Velasquez covers 75% and DHS capital funds cover the rest.

utterances.speaker: Erin Dalton
utterances.text: Shower privacy.

utterances.speaker: Erin Dalton
utterances.text: ICL is installing privacy partitions in all 32 showers.

utterances.speaker: Erin Dalton
utterances.text: The showers are in two areas of 15 and 17 each.

utterances.speaker: Erin Dalton
utterances.text: Each area will close in turn while partitions are installed so that the other areas stay open.

utterances.speaker: Erin Dalton
utterances.text: ICL expects the work to take six to eight weeks.

utterances.speaker: Erin Dalton
utterances.text: Residents also raise concern about the food at BAVR, and we take those concerns seriously.

utterances.speaker: Erin Dalton
utterances.text: ICL switched food vendors in 2022 in response to resident feedback, and in the coming weeks, DHS and ICL are exploring making additional changes in response to resident concerns.

utterances.speaker: Erin Dalton
utterances.text: In addition to responding to the smaller concerns related to the quality of food on site, we are also looking at opportunities with the on-site commercial kitchens.

utterances.speaker: Erin Dalton
utterances.text: Residents see what we see there, a commercial kitchen that is only used a few hours a day and not at all on weekends.

utterances.speaker: Erin Dalton
utterances.text: That kitchen is an opportunity.

utterances.speaker: Erin Dalton
utterances.text: DHS and ICL are exploring creative partnerships to make better use of it, including the potential to bring in military chefs to prepare special meals for residents.

utterances.speaker: Erin Dalton
utterances.text: That was a resident idea.

utterances.speaker: Erin Dalton
utterances.text: We are also looking at bigger changes to how food is prepared at BAVR.

utterances.speaker: Erin Dalton
utterances.text: Some of those changes will require procurement, and those discussions are just beginning.

utterances.speaker: Erin Dalton
utterances.text: We will keep residents informed as plans take shape.

chapters.summary: Dalton notes that AA, NA, and other on-site programs paused during COVID and never restarted, and says DHS is working to simplify the process for outside providers and volunteers to return to BAVR.
chapters.title: Dalton says on-site services paused during COVID are being restored

utterances.speaker: Erin Dalton
utterances.text: On-site services at Borden Avenue.

utterances.speaker: Erin Dalton
utterances.text: Some services that residents once relied on are no longer available in the building.

utterances.speaker: Erin Dalton
utterances.text: During COVID, several on-site programs were paused and never restarted, including Alcoholics Anonymous and Narcotics Anonymous.

utterances.speaker: Erin Dalton
utterances.text: Some DHS procedures have also made it harder for outside providers and volunteers to come on site.

utterances.speaker: Erin Dalton
utterances.text: We are working through these challenges.

utterances.speaker: Erin Dalton
utterances.text: We are committed to a simpler, faster process for bringing services back into the building without compromising residents'confidentiality or safety.

utterances.speaker: Erin Dalton
utterances.text: Our goal is to make it easy for trusted partners such as recovery group, veterans organizations, and community providers to meet residents where they live.

utterances.speaker: Erin Dalton
utterances.text: These services will add to the support already available on site, including employment and training programs, physical and mental health, and substance use services, and access to public benefits and permanent affordable housing.

utterances.speaker: Erin Dalton
utterances.text: We will continue to monitor building food and service conditions at BAVR.

chapters.summary: Dalton says Intro 897 would require outreach every two hours overnight and quarterly reports, and while DHS supports reporting, it has concerns about flexibility and the bill's alignment with the current Code Blue approach.
chapters.title: Dalton addresses Intro 897 on severe winter weather outreach

utterances.speaker: Erin Dalton
utterances.text: I will now turn to the legislation being discussed today.

utterances.speaker: Erin Dalton
utterances.text: Introduction 897.

utterances.speaker: Erin Dalton
utterances.text: sponsored by Councilmember Feliz would require best efforts for regular outreach work engagement every two hours between 8 p.m.

utterances.speaker: Erin Dalton
utterances.text: And 8 a.m.

utterances.speaker: Erin Dalton
utterances.text: During severe winter weather responses.

utterances.speaker: Erin Dalton
utterances.text: Coordinating with sister agencies on transportation, warming buses, warming centers, harm reduction facilities, as well as requiring four reports, one report prior to November, December, January, and February each winter on plans to implement the severe weather response.

utterances.speaker: Erin Dalton
utterances.text: We appreciate Council's focus on severe winter weather responses to ensure vulnerable New Yorkers are kept safe during the severe winter weather events.

utterances.speaker: Erin Dalton
utterances.text: We share this concern and focus.

utterances.speaker: Erin Dalton
utterances.text: Our severe weather response strategy is developed to incorporate lessons learned from prior Code Blue and Code Red responses.

utterances.speaker: Erin Dalton
utterances.text: The flexibility to implement lessons learned and revised strategies is critical to keeping New Yorkers safe during severe weather.

utterances.speaker: Erin Dalton
utterances.text: We hope to have substantive discussions with the sponsoring council to consider amendments to take into account a more comprehensive understanding of our current approach for Code Blue and the ongoing need to remain flexible when preparing for a severe weather event.

utterances.speaker: Erin Dalton
utterances.text: We have no concerns with the bill's proposal for regular reporting on Code Blue responses, but many of the other elements of the proposed legislation would require discussion.

utterances.speaker: Erin Dalton
utterances.text: The current language is based on DHS's previous approach, which centered on a list of known vulnerable clients who outreach teams would check on repeatedly during the weather event.

utterances.speaker: Erin Dalton
utterances.text: This is no longer the centerpiece of our response.

utterances.speaker: Erin Dalton
utterances.text: Every year, we will still identify the most vulnerable people on the street and make sure each one has a safety plan before winter.

chapters.summary: Dalton says DHS now canvasses all people on the street during extreme weather rather than only a known vulnerable list, tested during Code Red with over 2,000 engagements, and says the bill would limit this approach.
chapters.title: Dalton explains current Code Blue canvassing approach

utterances.speaker: Erin Dalton
utterances.text: But focusing only on that list leaves us without an approach for the roughly 5,000 other people on the street.

utterances.speaker: Erin Dalton
utterances.text: On the coldest nights and hottest nights of the year, the people we don't know may be at the greatest risk.

utterances.speaker: Erin Dalton
utterances.text: During the coldest nights of the year, additional canvassers will join DHS staff and contracted outreach teams to cover areas where we know most people experiencing unsheltered homelessness are staying.

utterances.speaker: Erin Dalton
utterances.text: These teams will engage everyone they encounter.

utterances.speaker: Erin Dalton
utterances.text: Everyone will be warned about the dangers of extreme weather and offered warming or cooling space, a shelter, a safe haven bed, another safe place to go with transportation to get there.

utterances.speaker: Erin Dalton
utterances.text: We tested this approach during Code Red, and looking at one day during Code Red this past summer, teams recorded more than 2,000 engagements with vulnerable people, roughly 20 times as many contacts and

utterances.speaker: Erin Dalton
utterances.text: seven times as many placements as on a comparable day under the old approach.

utterances.speaker: Erin Dalton
utterances.text: They handed out supplies to more than 1,500 people and completed nearly 200 medical assessments.

utterances.speaker: Erin Dalton
utterances.text: This approach will continue during Code Blue and is currently drafted.

utterances.speaker: Erin Dalton
utterances.text: The introduction would limit our ability to implement this approach effectively.

chapters.summary: Dalton says DSS is committed to quality care for veterans and will continue helping them find permanent affordable housing, thanks the council, and welcomes questions.
chapters.title: Dalton concludes DSS testimony and welcomes questions

utterances.speaker: Erin Dalton
utterances.text: DSS is committed to working with clients, shelter providers, elected officials, and our community stakeholders to continue to uphold our responsibility to serve veterans with the quality care they deserve.

utterances.speaker: Erin Dalton
utterances.text: DHS will continue to help to support them on their journey to stability with permanent and affordable housing that meets their individual needs.

utterances.speaker: Erin Dalton
utterances.text: These are men and women who serve this country.

utterances.speaker: Erin Dalton
utterances.text: They deserve nothing less than our best effort to help find stable, permanent, affordable housing.

utterances.speaker: Erin Dalton
utterances.text: Appreciate the council's leadership and attention to this work, and thank you for the opportunity to testify today and clear up any misunderstandings about the grant.

utterances.speaker: Erin Dalton
utterances.text: I welcome your questions.

chapters.summary: Morano asks why the city did not accept $1.3 million for 44 beds to reduce taxpayer burden; Dalton says the grant terms would violate state and local laws and, as a new agreement, could not be amended with objections.
chapters.title: Morano questions Dalton on declining VA grant funding

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: Thank you, Commissioners.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: And Commissioner Dalton, thank you especially for not only your testimony, but going out of your way to accommodate my colleagues and I in our visits to Borden Avenue and being patient with our questions and being receptive to resident feedback.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: Let me begin with discussion of the VA grant since it's been such a hot topic and since you alluded to that in your testimony.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: Your testimony says the VA offered the city $1.3 million to support 44 beds.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: Compared with the previous $4 million supporting 154 beds, right?

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: So I understand that you had objections to the federal conditions.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: Even if the city had to replace most of the funding with city dollars, wouldn't accepting $1.3 million still have reduced the burden on city taxpayers?

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: Did the administration explore accepting the federal funding for eligible beds while separately using city resources to ensure every other veteran continued receiving services?

utterances.speaker: Erin Dalton
utterances.text: Yeah, thank you for that question.

utterances.speaker: Erin Dalton
utterances.text: The challenge with the grants terms and conditions is that they would require us to be in violation of state and local laws.

utterances.speaker: Erin Dalton
utterances.text: And therefore, we could not sign that grant agreement and accept those dollars.

utterances.speaker: Erin Dalton
utterances.text: And therefore, we look for the city dollars to continue to serve every veteran that comes to our door.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: So there was no way to...

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: Accept the grant money and then, say, challenge the provisions that we believe are in violation of city and state law in court or something along those lines?

utterances.speaker: Erin Dalton
utterances.text: It's a little bit out of my legal expertise.

utterances.speaker: Erin Dalton
utterances.text: However, my understanding is that the difference here is that this was a new grant agreement.

utterances.speaker: Erin Dalton
utterances.text: When we had grant agreements and changes had been made, we could amend those and note our objections and continue and proceed in court.

utterances.speaker: Erin Dalton
utterances.text: But with this being a new grant agreement, we'd be signing on to those conditions from the beginning and therefore could not do that without violating state and local laws.

chapters.summary: Morano asks if veterans will live under tarps until 2029; Dalton says seven sleeping areas are offline, roof work starts June 2027, and she will look at expediting the timeline.
chapters.title: Morano presses Dalton on roof repair timeline and tarps

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: When time permits, if you could provide the committee with the legal analysis explaining why that arrangement wasn't permissible, I'd certainly appreciate it.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: I visited Borden Avenue a couple of weeks ago.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: I thought many aspects of the facility looked good, and I said so publicly.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: And honestly, given so many of the stories that we've heard from former Borden Avenue residents, I was...

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: quite frankly, expecting much worse.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: I was troubled by the leaks and the tarps, which you alluded to in your testimony.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: Your testimony said the $4.3 million roof and skylight replacement won't be completed until December of 2029.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: Are you telling us that veterans could be living in a shelter with tarps hanging over their sleeping areas for another three years?

utterances.speaker: Erin Dalton
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Erin Dalton
utterances.text: Thank you for the question.

utterances.speaker: Erin Dalton
utterances.text: So where there are tarps in the building, there are not veterans sleeping under those, right?

utterances.speaker: Erin Dalton
utterances.text: We are taking those sleeping areas offline.

utterances.speaker: Erin Dalton
utterances.text: Currently, I believe there are seven sleeping areas offline due to repairs being made to the roof.

utterances.speaker: Erin Dalton
utterances.text: But the construction process and procurement city process does give the timeline that I gave in my testimony,

utterances.speaker: Erin Dalton
utterances.text: which runs through December of 2029, but is expected to start in June of 2027.

utterances.speaker: Erin Dalton
utterances.text: So hopefully progress will be seen throughout that time.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: Is there anything that can be done to accelerate that timetable?

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: Maybe some sort of emergency procurement or any other way to eliminate the tarps at least a bit sooner?

utterances.speaker: Erin Dalton
utterances.text: I would certainly share that interest in expediting the timeline.

utterances.speaker: Erin Dalton
utterances.text: I can come back and see if there's anything we can do.

chapters.summary: Morano calls the barrack-style showers prison-like and asks for a hard date; Dalton says ICL will install partitions in six to eight weeks, with some showers completed earlier.
chapters.title: Morano questions Dalton on shower privacy timeline

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: alluded to the showers, and this is one thing that struck me during my visit, these barrack-style showers, almost like you'd see in a prison.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: I understand that many of these veterans served in the military, but obviously they're civilians now, and they deserve some privacy.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: Your testimony discusses shower improvements.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: This doesn't strike me as a multimillion-dollar project at all.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: Can you give us a hard and fast date of when every shower will offer reasonable privacy?

utterances.speaker: Erin Dalton
utterances.text: The best information I have available is that that work has been approved by us at the city, will be conducted by ICL, the provider, and has a timeline of six to eight weeks.

utterances.speaker: Erin Dalton
utterances.text: There is a process of taking some of those showers offline while those partitions are being constructed and then putting those back online and then doing the next set.

utterances.speaker: Erin Dalton
utterances.text: And so there will be...

utterances.speaker: Erin Dalton
utterances.text: There will be some showers that will have those partitions in place before the end of that timeline.

chapters.summary: Morano notes serious incidents dropped 44% and 911 calls dropped 48%, asking what changed; Russell attributes the decline to ICL collaboration, proactive meetings, and DHS on-site presence, and says reporting standards were unchanged.
chapters.title: Morano asks Dalton and Russell about incident decline causes

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: Your testimony reports that serious incidents at Borden Avenue declined 44% from 674 to 377, and 911 calls declined 48%

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: from 813 to 419.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: Those are very impressive numbers, and if they're accurate, I think the administration, including you, deserves a great deal of credit.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: But what specifically changed?

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: Was it staffing?

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: Was it security?

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: Was it programming?

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: Was it the resident population?

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: Was it how incidents were classified and reported?

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: It's great that we're seeing a decline in incidents.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: What do we attribute that to?

utterances.speaker: Erin Dalton
utterances.text: Sure.

utterances.speaker: Erin Dalton
utterances.text: I'm going to see if the deputy commissioner has any ideas about that.

utterances.speaker: Erin Dalton
utterances.text: But I don't think there have been changes in the way that the data is being recorded.

utterances.speaker: Sonia Russell
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: Sonia Russell
utterances.text: Again, Sonia Russell, Deputy Commissioner, Department of Homeless Services.

utterances.speaker: Sonia Russell
utterances.text: So thank you for that question.

utterances.speaker: Sonia Russell
utterances.text: It is a great question.

utterances.speaker: Sonia Russell
utterances.text: I would have to attribute that to ICL.

utterances.speaker: Sonia Russell
utterances.text: The fact that we work collectively and collaboratively with their staff and identifying incidences as soon as they happen or not to be reactive but proactive.

utterances.speaker: Sonia Russell
utterances.text: So that has to do with the common conversations that we have or consistent conversations that we have, the meetings that we have.

utterances.speaker: Sonia Russell
utterances.text: DHS is on site at Borden at least twice a week, if not once a week.

utterances.speaker: Sonia Russell
