utterances.speaker: Julie Won
utterances.text: From DSS or will that be coming from the Veterans Committee?

utterances.speaker: Julie Won
utterances.text: I mean, agency.

utterances.speaker: Julie Won
utterances.text: Which agency will the allotment be?

utterances.speaker: Erin Dalton
utterances.text: Yes, DHS is responsible for funding the shelters.

utterances.speaker: Erin Dalton
utterances.text: And we will release, of course, in a future financial plan, the exact expenses of the shelter over the next year.

utterances.speaker: Erin Dalton
utterances.text: But to reiterate.

utterances.speaker: Erin Dalton
utterances.text: DHS is covering the full cost of the shelter.

utterances.speaker: Julie Won
utterances.text: So could you say the amount?

utterances.speaker: Julie Won
utterances.text: Because currently in your testimony, it only says the 1.3 million.

utterances.speaker: Julie Won
utterances.text: We have been alerted by the veterans that it's a shortage of 4 million total that is the differential from previous year's funding to now for this shelter.

utterances.speaker: Erin Dalton
utterances.text: Yeah, the numbers are a little bit confusing, right?

utterances.speaker: Erin Dalton
utterances.text: So the grant was covering 154 beds, and we could claim up to $4 million, right?

utterances.speaker: Erin Dalton
utterances.text: So the way this works at the city level is the city pays up front for the cost of the shelter, and then we claim as much federal dollars as we can, right?

utterances.speaker: Erin Dalton
utterances.text: And so the grant allowed us to claim for up to 154 beds and up to $4 million, right?

utterances.speaker: Erin Dalton
utterances.text: The revised award, if we had accepted it, would allow us to claim for up to 44 beds and up to $1.3 million.

utterances.speaker: Erin Dalton
utterances.text: And as I said, we will report out as we do and as OMB always does the expenses as we move into the next year.

utterances.speaker: Erin Dalton
utterances.text: But we are committed to cover it, and it's DHS.

utterances.speaker: Erin Dalton
utterances.text: and not Department of Veterans Services, who will be covering the entire cost.

utterances.speaker: Julie Won
utterances.text: Okay, thank you for the clarification.

chapters.summary: Won reports veterans complain of malnutrition, no kitchen access, and food confiscation; Dalton says no shelter allows cooking, and Russell says food standards are monitored, microwaves may be added, and outside food can be eaten in the cafeteria.
chapters.title: Won questions Dalton and Russell on food quality and kitchen access

utterances.speaker: Julie Won
utterances.text: I just have one last question.

utterances.speaker: Julie Won
utterances.text: Could you help me understand about the lack of nutrients and food that is available?

utterances.speaker: Julie Won
utterances.text: And this is not an individual shelter problem for ICL at Borden Avenue, but I hear this also for other ICL shelters in my district in Long Island City.

utterances.speaker: Julie Won
utterances.text: What is happening?

utterances.speaker: Julie Won
utterances.text: Because I'm also hearing conflicting information from what Chair Hudson just testified or put on record about the use of kitchen because we have multiple veterans that complain to my office that they have no kitchen access whatsoever, that they're not allowed to bring outside food into the shelter.

utterances.speaker: Julie Won
utterances.text: And also hundreds of them will continue to say that they have malnutrition because they're not getting enough food.

utterances.speaker: Julie Won
utterances.text: So can you help us understand what's going on with the current kitchen usage as well as their diet, their food and nutrients?

utterances.speaker: Julie Won
utterances.text: And what is the per diem per meal per day so that we can get a very...

utterances.speaker: Julie Won
utterances.text: Clear understanding of what is the caloric nutrient requirement per meal for ICL at the shelter for a grown man.

utterances.speaker: Erin Dalton
utterances.text: Yes, thank you.

utterances.speaker: Erin Dalton
utterances.text: And thank you to Chair Hudson for doing important clarifications that I had not done.

utterances.speaker: Erin Dalton
utterances.text: And I will, before this question ends, I would like to turn it over to the Deputy Commissioner to add any detail.

utterances.speaker: Erin Dalton
utterances.text: And we may need to, we'll see, we may need to get back to you on exactly what

utterances.speaker: Erin Dalton
utterances.text: what those per diems are.

utterances.speaker: Erin Dalton
utterances.text: But I agree with Chair Hudson there.

utterances.speaker: Erin Dalton
utterances.text: This is a bit of a systemic issue, right?

utterances.speaker: Erin Dalton
utterances.text: The issue of food and the quality of food in our shelters is governed by a number of different rules, including the New York City health and safety standards and food standards that we must comply with.

utterances.speaker: Erin Dalton
utterances.text: And we do monitor too.

utterances.speaker: Erin Dalton
utterances.text: So that monitoring is happening.

utterances.speaker: Erin Dalton
utterances.text: The chair is correct that in no shelter across the Department of Homeless Services system are people permitted to cook their own food.

utterances.speaker: Erin Dalton
utterances.text: That said, I've not visited nearly as many shelters as I would like to, but in my time here, which has only been a couple of months, but I've visited a number of shelters, and there is variation here, right?

utterances.speaker: Erin Dalton
utterances.text: For example, Chair Hudson and I talked to somebody last night who had just been at a different shelter and was talking about the food quality differential.

utterances.speaker: Erin Dalton
utterances.text: I do think, as I've testified to and answered questions about, that we can do more to improve the food quality at Vorden in particular, and that there are other systemic issues that we do need to look at in terms of the food.

utterances.speaker: Erin Dalton
utterances.text: I will turn it over to the Deputy Commissioner to see if she has anything additional to add there.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: Commissioner, it actually does seem like your mic is a bit low.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: I'm not sure if that's a volume issue or if it's a facing the mic issue.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Sonia Russell
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: Sonia Russell
utterances.text: So just to piggyback on what Commissioner Dalton indicated is that, yes, we are.

utterances.speaker: Sonia Russell
utterances.text: required not only at Borden, but across the entire shelter system to follow New York City, the food standards.

utterances.speaker: Sonia Russell
utterances.text: So that monitors the caloric intake, sodium, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: Sonia Russell
utterances.text: So I absolutely agree with Chair Hudson with respect to the

utterances.speaker: Sonia Russell
utterances.text: small juices that our veterans or our clients receive.

utterances.speaker: Sonia Russell
utterances.text: But we are having conversations internally, but also with ICL on how we can help that as well or augment that.

utterances.speaker: Sonia Russell
utterances.text: So at some of our shelters, we do have microwaves in the cafeteria, which would allow a client to come in and let's say if they want to heat some food up that they purchased from outside, they can do so.

utterances.speaker: Sonia Russell
utterances.text: With respect to cooking, you know, I definitely want to be clear that we don't allow cooking at our shelter residence for single men or women.

utterances.speaker: Sonia Russell
utterances.text: But again, if a client wants to bring in food and they want to eat it in the cafeteria, this would be permissible during the cafeteria hours.

utterances.speaker: Sonia Russell
utterances.text: And again, if they want to use microwaves, we can have conversations with Borden on how we can help make that possible.

utterances.speaker: Julie Won
utterances.text: Can you help me understand?

utterances.speaker: Julie Won
utterances.text: So to be clear, you're saying that they can bring outside food into the shelter and it won't be confiscated by the staff of ICL?

utterances.speaker: Sonia Russell
utterances.text: So, I mean, we have to, client have to bring in the food and the staff will have to escort them to the cafeteria to ensure that they're not eating in the dorms.

utterances.speaker: Sonia Russell
utterances.text: We don't want to create an issue of rodents.

utterances.speaker: Sonia Russell
utterances.text: So, yes, it's having conversations with ICL and with other providers if they are not allowing this to happen.

utterances.speaker: Sonia Russell
utterances.text: then these are conversations we can have with our providers.

utterances.speaker: Julie Won
utterances.text: I think that will be necessary because we get reports that their food is confiscated if they bring outside food because they're still hungry.

utterances.speaker: Sonia Russell
utterances.text: I thank you for bringing that to our attention, and that is a conversation that we will have with ICL leadership.

chapters.summary: Won raises a conflict of interest in the cooking class contract and asks how many veterans can participate; Russell says slots are set aside, does not know the number, and says the food vendor is Healthy Beets.
chapters.title: Won questions culinary program slots and food vendor

utterances.speaker: Julie Won
utterances.text: So for the cooking class that is happening, it was also brought to our attention that the cooking class contract is to the former organization where the CEO used to work.

utterances.speaker: Julie Won
utterances.text: So that seems like a conflict of interest.

utterances.speaker: Julie Won
utterances.text: But in addition to that, can you please help me understand?

utterances.speaker: Julie Won
utterances.text: The cooking class is not intended for the veterans who is resident to the building.

utterances.speaker: Julie Won
utterances.text: It is only for outsiders.

utterances.speaker: Sonia Russell
utterances.text: No, that's incorrect.

utterances.speaker: Phil Wong
utterances.text: Councilmember Wong brought that up as well.

utterances.speaker: Sonia Russell
utterances.text: Yes, so that's incorrect.

utterances.speaker: Sonia Russell
utterances.text: We have set aside slots for the veterans to participate in the cooking class if they wish to do so.

utterances.speaker: Julie Won
utterances.text: So how many veterans can participate versus how many are actual residents there?

utterances.speaker: Julie Won
utterances.text: Because it seems like many of them want to be able to cook their food because they're dissatisfied with the quality of food that they're receiving.

utterances.speaker: Julie Won
utterances.text: Many of them tell us that it's mostly beans of some kind and just rice or some sort of carb.

utterances.speaker: Sonia Russell
utterances.text: So I want to just be clear.

utterances.speaker: Sonia Russell
utterances.text: So as far as cooking their meals, the veterans cannot cook their meals.

utterances.speaker: Sonia Russell
utterances.text: With respect to participating in the culinary program, we do have slots that are available for those veterans that reside.

utterances.speaker: Julie Won
utterances.text: So how many slots?

utterances.speaker: Sonia Russell
utterances.text: Unfortunately, I don't have that number.

utterances.speaker: Sonia Russell
utterances.text: It might be 10 slots.

utterances.speaker: Julie Won
utterances.text: Because my point is that the ratio of slots available.

utterances.speaker: Julie Won
utterances.text: versus the residents who want to participate is not enough.

utterances.speaker: Julie Won
utterances.text: And if people outside with the shelter are being able to give, are given access to this cooking class, yet the residents themselves are not, that is a point of conflict and tension for them.

utterances.speaker: Sonia Russell
utterances.text: So we don't have reports that indicate that veterans are being turned away from the program or not able to participate in the program.

utterances.speaker: Sonia Russell
utterances.text: But again, if that's information that you have and you're willing to share, by all means, we'll be happy to look into it.

utterances.speaker: Sonia Russell
utterances.text: But we will have conversations with ICL because, again, our veterans are allowed to participate in the program.

utterances.speaker: Sonia Russell
utterances.text: Culinary program because I myself made that clear when we negotiated this that those that are at boarding can participate and will participate thank you as long as they have the time in which to do so.

utterances.speaker: Julie Won
utterances.text: Okay but 10 slots is not enough for the number of beds that we have.

utterances.speaker: Julie Won
utterances.text: I promise we'll come back to you.

utterances.speaker: Julie Won
utterances.text: Can I just have one last question who is the contractor for the food at the site?

utterances.speaker: Sonia Russell
utterances.text: I believe that is Project Renewal.

utterances.speaker: Sonia Russell
utterances.text: Oh, healthy beets.

utterances.speaker: Sonia Russell
utterances.text: I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: Sonia Russell
utterances.text: I thought you said the culinary.

utterances.speaker: Julie Won
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: Sonia Russell
utterances.text: The food vendor is healthy beets.

utterances.speaker: Sonia Russell
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: Julie Won
utterances.text: For all three meals per day.

utterances.speaker: Julie Won
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: Julie Won
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

chapters.summary: Morano asks how many transgender veterans are in NYC or at Borden; Dalton says some exist but she does not have numbers, Mata says self-identification is an issue, and Orlando says there is no exact number.
chapters.title: Morano asks Dalton and Mata about transgender veteran count

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: I have one quick question before we go back to Councilmember Wong.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: Going back to the grant issue, a lot of this seems to have to do with the federal government having a policy which was at odds with city and state policy regarding trans veterans and things of that nature.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: And I understand that it's the city and the state's policy.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: I am curious, though, how many...

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: trans veterans there are either in New York City or at Borden Avenue.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: Just to, I understand it wouldn't affect the policy decision to reject the grant money, but I think the public is curious just about how many folks that would affect.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: Ballpark, if you have.

utterances.speaker: Erin Dalton
utterances.text: Thanks.

utterances.speaker: Erin Dalton
utterances.text: And I don't...

utterances.speaker: Erin Dalton
utterances.text: My colleagues at DVS may want to also answer because your question was broader than the shelter system.

utterances.speaker: Erin Dalton
utterances.text: What I can tell you is that we do know of veterans who identify as transgender or gender nonconforming in our shelter system.

utterances.speaker: Erin Dalton
utterances.text: And I don't have the numbers, but we know that does exist.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: Is there a ballpark number in the shelter system?

utterances.speaker: Erin Dalton
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: Erin Dalton
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: Yesenia Mata
utterances.text: Just to further elaborate, I'll pass that question to my chief of staff, Nicole.

utterances.speaker: Yesenia Mata
utterances.text: Self-identification, as we have mentioned plenty of times in past hearings, has been an issue.

utterances.speaker: Yesenia Mata
utterances.text: And at DBS, we are doing the best that we can when it comes to providing that outreach support to ensure that specifically when it comes to the LGBT community, they can self-identify.

utterances.speaker: Yesenia Mata
utterances.text: And I'll let Nicole further.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: Before you answer, Ms.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: Orlando, I am having a tough time hearing all the witnesses at the witness table.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: And I see that their mic is on, and I see they're speaking directly into it.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: I don't know if that's an audio issue that we can resolve.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: But fortunately, I know Ms.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: Orlando can project.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: Nicole Orlando
utterances.text: Thank you for the question and thank you to all committee that are here today.

utterances.speaker: Nicole Orlando
utterances.text: For us, we don't have an exact number for transgender veterans that are here in New York City largely.

utterances.speaker: Nicole Orlando
utterances.text: Looking back to our testimony that we provided in the LGBTQ plus hearing, we are working, as Commissioner mentioned, to make sure that a veteran feels comfortable enough to self-identify, as well as looking into what benefits are provided.

utterances.speaker: Nicole Orlando
utterances.text: So we would be happy to keep you updated with the identification piece of this.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: Council Member Wong.

chapters.summary: Wong asks why veterans need bottles next to their beds; Dalton says no one reported bathroom safety issues, the bathrooms are typical, and the shower privacy concerns are being fixed.
chapters.title: Wong questions Dalton on urine bottles and bathroom safety

utterances.speaker: Phil Wong
utterances.text: Thank you, Chair.

utterances.speaker: Phil Wong
utterances.text: Commissioner Dalton, can you explain why veterans would need to have bottles next to their beds so they could urinate into, even though the bathroom is a short walk away?

utterances.speaker: Phil Wong
utterances.text: Like, what is the issue?

utterances.speaker: Phil Wong
utterances.text: Is the bathroom not safe?

utterances.speaker: Phil Wong
utterances.text: Or is there some, why would you even allow that to happen?

utterances.speaker: Erin Dalton
utterances.text: Yeah, no, thank you for the opportunity to clarify.

utterances.speaker: Erin Dalton
utterances.text: And while I did not speak with every veteran who is residing at Borden Avenue, I spent, I don't know, 90 minutes or so with a number of folks and have been there over a couple of times over the past couple of weeks and talked to others as well.

utterances.speaker: Erin Dalton
utterances.text: And nobody has reported to me about safety in the bathroom.

utterances.speaker: Erin Dalton
utterances.text: We certainly have heard about the showers where there are real privacy concerns that I agree with and we are fixing.

utterances.speaker: Erin Dalton
utterances.text: But the actual bathrooms I've seen myself and are typical bathrooms.

utterances.speaker: Erin Dalton
utterances.text: Nobody reported that they were nervous or unable to use the bathroom.

utterances.speaker: Erin Dalton
utterances.text: I think that that notice was just a notice that got put out.

chapters.summary: Wong asks if DHS attends CAP meetings; Russell says yes, and Wong says residents raised issues with no action, says veterans want to cook because they are hungry, and criticizes culinary school access.
chapters.title: Wong questions DHS attendance at CAP meetings and food access

utterances.speaker: Phil Wong
utterances.text: Yeah, it seemed to me that the

utterances.speaker: Phil Wong
utterances.text: HHS should have people there at these CAP meetings, and they should be well aware of these issues that we're discussing today.

utterances.speaker: Phil Wong
utterances.text: My question, do you have someone attending these CAP meetings?

utterances.speaker: Phil Wong
utterances.text: Please answer.

utterances.speaker: Erin Dalton
utterances.text: Yeah, yeah.

utterances.speaker: Erin Dalton
utterances.text: I will turn it over to the deputy commissioner to answer.

utterances.speaker: Sonia Russell
utterances.text: So, yes, to answer your question, we do have DHS staff that attends the CAP meetings.

utterances.speaker: Phil Wong
utterances.text: Yeah, but I'm sure these issues were brought up many times because I was told by the residents that they would discuss in CAP meetings and nothing was done or

utterances.speaker: Phil Wong
utterances.text: addressed, is not being addressed, such as not enough food.

utterances.speaker: Phil Wong
utterances.text: Look, if there's enough food, nobody will bother wanting to cook there.

utterances.speaker: Phil Wong
utterances.text: The reason they want to cook there is because they're hungry.

utterances.speaker: Phil Wong
utterances.text: And it's unacceptable to me that you allow the people in the cooking school to cook, but the veterans there cannot cook.

utterances.speaker: Phil Wong
utterances.text: Think about that.

utterances.speaker: Phil Wong
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: Phil Wong
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: Phil Wong
utterances.text: Follow-up question.

utterances.speaker: Phil Wong
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: Phil Wong
utterances.text: Follow-up question.

utterances.speaker: Phil Wong
utterances.text: All right.

chapters.summary: Wong asks for a breakdown of the 419 911 calls; Dalton says many are medical and will provide a breakdown.
chapters.title: Wong requests breakdown of 911 calls at Borden

utterances.speaker: Phil Wong
utterances.text: Your testimony said there are 259 911 calls.

utterances.speaker: Phil Wong
utterances.text: Sorry.

utterances.speaker: Phil Wong
utterances.text: No, I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: Phil Wong
utterances.text: 419 911 calls.

utterances.speaker: Phil Wong
utterances.text: Can you give a breakdown?

utterances.speaker: Phil Wong
utterances.text: Like what are the issues that you're dealing with?

utterances.speaker: Phil Wong
utterances.text: In the Board and Avenue site?

utterances.speaker: Erin Dalton
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: Erin Dalton
utterances.text: I may be able to pull them up for you in this time frame, and I may have to report back in a couple minutes as I look for it.

utterances.speaker: Erin Dalton
utterances.text: I will say in general terms, a lot of calls, which you could see in my testimony, are down, are related to medical care, right?

utterances.speaker: Erin Dalton
utterances.text: People, veterans, others experience medical emergencies just like everybody else, and there are 911 calls for those kinds of issues.

utterances.speaker: Erin Dalton
utterances.text: But if you will allow me a few.

utterances.speaker: Erin Dalton
utterances.text: Yes, I would like to see a breakdown of the 911 calls.

utterances.speaker: Erin Dalton
utterances.text: Absolutely.

utterances.speaker: Erin Dalton
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Erin Dalton
utterances.text: We can provide that.

utterances.speaker: Phil Wong
utterances.text: Please.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: Thank you, Councilmember Wong.

chapters.summary: Morano asks how long a roof repair would take in Pennsylvania; Dalton says she shares the concern, a new DHS administrator is reviewing the process, and they will look to expedite.
chapters.title: Morano asks Dalton about capital project timelines

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: Before I turn it back to Chair Hudson, Commissioner Dalton, I do want to take advantage of your Pennsylvania perspective for something.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: You know, one of the few areas that I think all 51 of my colleagues agree on is that we're frustrated at the pace of New York City capital projects.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: And I'm just still trying to wrap my head around the fact that

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: It's going to take three years to fix a leaking roof.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: When you were in Pennsylvania, how long would it take to fix a roof there?

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: Not three years, I'm betting.

utterances.speaker: Erin Dalton
utterances.text: Yeah, I do not have roof estimates from Pennsylvania.

utterances.speaker: Erin Dalton
utterances.text: But I, oh, look, that's working now.

utterances.speaker: Erin Dalton
utterances.text: There you go.

utterances.speaker: Erin Dalton
utterances.text: See?

utterances.speaker: Erin Dalton
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: Erin Dalton
utterances.text: However, I share the concern about how long things take and our responsiveness.

utterances.speaker: Erin Dalton
utterances.text: We have a new DHS administrator, Risa Henderson, and she and I both are looking at the process.

utterances.speaker: Erin Dalton
utterances.text: There's, of course, a citywide process that has a planning procedure that is required and funding procedure that is required.

utterances.speaker: Erin Dalton
utterances.text: But then there's also the piece on our side.

utterances.speaker: Erin Dalton
utterances.text: How are we managing those dollars?

utterances.speaker: Erin Dalton
utterances.text: How are we prioritizing them?

utterances.speaker: Erin Dalton
utterances.text: How are we procuring?

utterances.speaker: Erin Dalton
utterances.text: And we're looking at that entire process from bottom to top to see what we can do to expedite.

utterances.speaker: Erin Dalton
utterances.text: We don't like to see our buildings in disrepair and our people struggling under those.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: Well, let us know how we can help.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: I think, you know, not speaking for the mayor or the speaker, but I can tell you everybody up here and all the members of my committee, we're committed to doing everything in our purview to making sure that we can help reduce that timeline.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: Chair Hudson.

chapters.summary: Hudson reads social services law 136 and city charter section 29, argues the law protects personally identifying information, and says the council has authority to investigate and should be able to make unannounced visits.
chapters.title: Hudson cites city charter oversight authority over shelter visits

utterances.speaker: Crystal Hudson
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Crystal Hudson
utterances.text: I, you know, I am going to belabor the point of the.

utterances.speaker: Crystal Hudson
utterances.text: the NDA piece, the state law that I believe you referenced, social services law 136, was that it?

utterances.speaker: Crystal Hudson
utterances.text: Is that accurate?

utterances.speaker: Crystal Hudson
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: Crystal Hudson
utterances.text: Because that is the protection of public welfare records.

utterances.speaker: Crystal Hudson
utterances.text: And the first line says the names or addresses of persons applying for or receiving public assistance and care shall not be included

utterances.speaker: Crystal Hudson
utterances.text: in any published report or printed in any newspaper or reported at any public meeting except meetings of the county, blah, blah, blah.

utterances.speaker: Crystal Hudson
utterances.text: And so that seems to me to be very specific to names and addresses or privacy, personally identifying information for individuals.

utterances.speaker: Crystal Hudson
utterances.text: Whereas in the city charter section 29, under power of investigation and oversight,

utterances.speaker: Crystal Hudson
utterances.text: It states that the council, acting as a committee of the whole and each standing or special committee of the council,

utterances.speaker: Crystal Hudson
utterances.text: through hearings or otherwise, may investigate any matters within its jurisdiction relating to the property,

utterances.speaker: Crystal Hudson
utterances.text: affairs, or government of the city or of any county within the city or to any other powers of the council or to the effectuation of the purposes or provisions of this charter or any laws relating to the city

utterances.speaker: Crystal Hudson
utterances.text: or to any county within the city.

utterances.speaker: Crystal Hudson
utterances.text: Now, I'm not an attorney.

utterances.speaker: Crystal Hudson
utterances.text: I know you're not an attorney, so maybe we can let our attorneys or respective attorneys hash it out.

utterances.speaker: Crystal Hudson
utterances.text: But my interpretation of this is that we have the authority as members of the

utterances.speaker: Crystal Hudson
utterances.text: this body to investigate any matters, as it says, within its jurisdiction relating to the property of any city agency.

utterances.speaker: Crystal Hudson
utterances.text: And I think the law that you referenced is specific to personally identifying records.

utterances.speaker: Crystal Hudson
utterances.text: And I would also argue that as council members who provide constituent services every day in our offices,

utterances.speaker: Crystal Hudson
utterances.text: We are not sharing personally identifying information, and we have stopgaps and practices and policies within the body that prevent us from sharing and

utterances.speaker: Crystal Hudson
utterances.text: personally identifying information for those who we serve every single day.

utterances.speaker: Crystal Hudson
utterances.text: So I would argue that we should have.

utterances.speaker: Crystal Hudson
utterances.text: The authority and the ability to make unannounced visits to shelters.

utterances.speaker: Crystal Hudson
utterances.text: And I know we did one last night, but fully and truly unannounced the way we see it as duly elected council members.

utterances.speaker: Crystal Hudson
utterances.text: So I just wanted to make that point.

chapters.summary: Hudson asks what equitable access looks like for women, LGBTQ+, older, and disabled veterans and whether veterans can choose a different shelter; Mata describes outreach with other agencies, roundtables, and DVS as a connector.
chapters.title: Hudson asks Mata about equitable access and shelter options

utterances.speaker: Crystal Hudson
utterances.text: And then I wanted to, for Commissioner Mata,

utterances.speaker: Crystal Hudson
utterances.text: You referenced in your testimony strengthening equitable access for women veterans, LGBTQ plus veterans, older veterans, veterans with disabilities, and communities that may face additional barriers to services.

utterances.speaker: Crystal Hudson
utterances.text: Can you just share what that looks like?

utterances.speaker: Crystal Hudson
utterances.text: And if someone prefers to be in a different type of shelter environment, what that process looks like if they didn't want to be at somewhere like a Borden Avenue?

utterances.speaker: Crystal Hudson
utterances.text: And also on the website, it says that Borden Avenue houses both male and female veterans.

utterances.speaker: Crystal Hudson
utterances.text: Can you verify?

utterances.speaker: Crystal Hudson
utterances.text: Whether that's accurate?

utterances.speaker: Yesenia Mata
utterances.text: When it comes to Borden, I will defer the questions to Commissioner Delton.

utterances.speaker: Yesenia Mata
utterances.text: There's two answers to that.

utterances.speaker: Yesenia Mata
utterances.text: First, to the component of the outreaching that we are doing when it comes to women veterans, LGBTQ plus veterans, and veterans with disabilities.

utterances.speaker: Yesenia Mata
utterances.text: We are working in conjunction with other city agencies, such as the Commissioner for Disability, the Commissioner of Aging,

utterances.speaker: Yesenia Mata
utterances.text: to ensure that we have a collaborative effort to outreach properly to those veterans.

utterances.speaker: Yesenia Mata
utterances.text: We also have held various roundtables to ensure that we can hear directly from the veteran groups as to how we should be outreaching.

utterances.speaker: Yesenia Mata
utterances.text: Further, we also want to thank City Council for...

utterances.speaker: Yesenia Mata
utterances.text: when it comes to outreaching and more information is going to come out on that.

utterances.speaker: Yesenia Mata
utterances.text: We just finalized that specific plan.

utterances.speaker: Yesenia Mata
utterances.text: And I will further refer this to my chief of staff, Nicole.

utterances.speaker: Yesenia Mata
utterances.text: But at DBS, further what we are doing when it

utterances.speaker: Yesenia Mata
utterances.text: Our main focus is to be the sole connector.

utterances.speaker: Yesenia Mata
utterances.text: So what we do is our focus is to place veterans into housing, and that is a very rigorous process at the agency.

utterances.speaker: Yesenia Mata
utterances.text: We assess the needs.

utterances.speaker: Yesenia Mata
utterances.text: We develop individualized housing plans, help identify units, arrange viewings, gather documents, coordinate subsidies and inspections with the responsible agencies, and provide the aftercare component.

utterances.speaker: Yesenia Mata
utterances.text: So after Nicole explains further the outreach, Donnie Smalls will go further on the aftercare.

utterances.speaker: Nicole Orlando
utterances.text: Thank you so much again for that question.

utterances.speaker: Nicole Orlando
utterances.text: And just to emphasize Commissioner Mata's response, as well as we're really focused in this administration under the leadership of Commissioner Mata on veteran feedback on a lot of programming and things that we are doing.

utterances.speaker: Nicole Orlando
utterances.text: This includes the inclusion on our website of a feedback form that a veteran can fill out if they have issues with any aspect that's going on in the veteran community.

utterances.speaker: Nicole Orlando
utterances.text: This helps us to identify what these issues are and being able to better support, as well as Commissioner mentioned, the collaboration with different city agencies, city council members, so that we can all be in constant communication about these issues otherwise, as well as ideas that veterans have.

utterances.speaker: Nicole Orlando
utterances.text: So that includes roundtable discussions, partnership with our independent board, and just understanding what the community needs.

utterances.speaker: Nicole Orlando
utterances.text: I'll pass over to Dane.

chapters.summary: Smalls says the aftercare team maintains contact with housed veterans, identifies concerns early, and connects them to services.
chapters.title: Smalls describes DVS aftercare and housing stability work

utterances.speaker: Donnie Smalls
utterances.text: Thank you for that question.

utterances.speaker: Donnie Smalls
utterances.text: For the aftercare component, our team supports housing stability and homelessness prevention by maintaining contact with housed veterans and connecting them to services.

utterances.speaker: Donnie Smalls
utterances.text: Scheduled contacts help identify concerns early, urgent housing needs, and address as they arise and are more limited to scheduled intervals.

chapters.summary: Hudson asks about women at Borden; Russell says it was co-ed until 2018, is now all male, and women were transferred to another ICL facility; Hudson asks that the website be updated.
chapters.title: Hudson asks about women at Borden, Russell says facility is all male

utterances.speaker: Crystal Hudson
utterances.text: Thank you all.

utterances.speaker: Crystal Hudson
utterances.text: And then Commissioner Dalton, yeah, or Deputy Commissioner.

utterances.speaker: Crystal Hudson
utterances.text: I'm speaking to this.

utterances.speaker: Crystal Hudson
utterances.text: There's not women there.

utterances.speaker: Sonia Russell
utterances.text: Yes, I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: Sonia Russell
utterances.text: Yes, years ago it was a co-ed facility, but on about 2018, I believe when we started with the GPD grant, we switched to all males and the women were transferred to another facility under ICL.

utterances.speaker: Crystal Hudson
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: Crystal Hudson
utterances.text: I would encourage you to update the website.

utterances.speaker: Sonia Russell
utterances.text: Thank you.

chapters.summary: Hudson notes a 44% decline from 2015 to 2025 but a rise from 482 in 2022 to 697 in 2025 and asks about factors and strategies; Dalton cites a 93% decline in federal VASH vouchers and says federal disinvestment is hurting progress.
chapters.title: Hudson asks Dalton about rise in veteran homelessness

utterances.speaker: Crystal Hudson
utterances.text: Okay, although New York City reduced veteran homelessness by approximately 44% between 2015 and 2025, the number of homeless veterans has increased in recent years,

utterances.speaker: Crystal Hudson
utterances.text: rising from 482 individuals in 2022 to 697 in 2025.

utterances.speaker: Crystal Hudson
utterances.text: What factors have contributed to this increase?

utterances.speaker: Crystal Hudson
utterances.text: What specific strategies is the administration implementing to reverse this trend?

utterances.speaker: Crystal Hudson
utterances.text: And additionally, what policies, programs, or investments were most responsible for the significant reductions achieved between 2015 and 2022?

utterances.speaker: Crystal Hudson
utterances.text: And how is the administration?

utterances.speaker: Crystal Hudson
utterances.text: building upon those successes today.

utterances.speaker: Erin Dalton
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Erin Dalton
utterances.text: I'll start, and my colleagues may very well want to jump in here.

utterances.speaker: Erin Dalton
utterances.text: And I think, you know, it was a tremendous decline in veteran homelessness across the country.

utterances.speaker: Erin Dalton
utterances.text: And I think what you saw from both at a national level and federal level, as well as here in New York City, is people just doing the things that they needed to do, providing the vouchers that they needed, prioritizing this population, bringing them into shelter

utterances.speaker: Erin Dalton
utterances.text: when that was part of the journey and helping them to move on to housing quickly.

utterances.speaker: Erin Dalton
utterances.text: I will say that all of us should be encouraging.

utterances.speaker: Erin Dalton
utterances.text: Federal investments to be restored for this group.

utterances.speaker: Erin Dalton
utterances.text: The federal VASH vouchers, which I think in our previous history here were a good percentage of the way people left the homelessness system on that voucher, have declined deeply over the past few years.

utterances.speaker: Erin Dalton
utterances.text: And so while the current veterans who are on those vouchers, the feds will say are safe on them, the decline for new vouchers has dropped.

utterances.speaker: Erin Dalton
utterances.text: I have

utterances.speaker: Erin Dalton
utterances.text: Hold on, 93% from its peak.

utterances.speaker: Erin Dalton
utterances.text: So the federal government is really leaving us without specific housing resources for this population.

utterances.speaker: Erin Dalton
utterances.text: So we as a city are the most...

utterances.speaker: Erin Dalton
utterances.text: most generous in the country in terms of providing local funding for rental assistance and payment and support for people exiting homelessness, including the veterans population.

utterances.speaker: Erin Dalton
utterances.text: And New York City, again, supports veterans and sees them as eligible entities, whether they are in shelter or in community for programs like CityFAPS.

utterances.speaker: Erin Dalton
utterances.text: And so I would say the federal disinvestment or the federal investment really helped us to reduce homelessness during that period.

utterances.speaker: Erin Dalton
utterances.text: And the federal disinvestment is hurting our ability to continue to have those strides.

utterances.speaker: Erin Dalton
utterances.text: I will say New York City still has one of the lowest or the lowest veteran homelessness in the country.

utterances.speaker: Erin Dalton
utterances.text: We find, thankfully, very few people on the street who identify, self-identify as a veteran.

utterances.speaker: Erin Dalton
utterances.text: And so to the extent to which folks are homeless here, they are in our shelter system.

utterances.speaker: Erin Dalton
utterances.text: But I would encourage all of us to look at the federal government for the support that we need to serve this group.

chapters.summary: Hudson asks which boroughs have the highest concentrations; Dalton gives Bronx 24%, Brooklyn 23%, Manhattan 21%, Queens 12%, Staten Island 2%, and 17% with no verifiable address; Orlando adds districts 14, 15, and 31.
chapters.title: Hudson asks Dalton about borough concentrations of homeless veterans

utterances.speaker: Crystal Hudson
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Crystal Hudson
utterances.text: And which boroughs, council districts, or neighborhoods have the highest concentrations of veterans experiencing homelessness, and how is the city targeting outreach and services to those highest need areas?

utterances.speaker: Erin Dalton
utterances.text: Yeah, thank you.

utterances.speaker: Erin Dalton
utterances.text: So I can answer the question for folks who were in shelter in September of this year, their last address, right?

utterances.speaker: Erin Dalton
utterances.text: So I think that gets to the answer to your question.

utterances.speaker: Crystal Hudson
utterances.text: So that's a borough breakdown?

utterances.speaker: Erin Dalton
utterances.text: Yep, a borough breakdown.

utterances.speaker: Erin Dalton
utterances.text: Bronx, 24%.

utterances.speaker: Erin Dalton
utterances.text: Brooklyn, 23%.

utterances.speaker: Erin Dalton
utterances.text: Manhattan, 21%.

utterances.speaker: Erin Dalton
utterances.text: Queens, 12%.

utterances.speaker: Erin Dalton
utterances.text: Staten Island, 2%.

utterances.speaker: Erin Dalton
utterances.text: We've got unknown ad or unknown.

utterances.speaker: Crystal Hudson
utterances.text: Sorry, Manhattan was 23%.

utterances.speaker: Crystal Hudson
utterances.text: Queens was 12%.

utterances.speaker: Erin Dalton
utterances.text: Sorry, I'll start again.

utterances.speaker: Erin Dalton
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: Erin Dalton
utterances.text: Bronx, 24%.

utterances.speaker: Erin Dalton
utterances.text: Brooklyn, 23%.

utterances.speaker: Erin Dalton
utterances.text: Manhattan, 21%.

utterances.speaker: Erin Dalton
utterances.text: Queens, 12%.

utterances.speaker: Erin Dalton
utterances.text: Staten Island, 2%.

utterances.speaker: Erin Dalton
utterances.text: We do have 17% with no verifiable associated New York City address.

utterances.speaker: Erin Dalton
utterances.text: And only 1% with an unknown prior address other than shelter.

utterances.speaker: Crystal Hudson
utterances.text: Okay, great.

utterances.speaker: Crystal Hudson
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Nicole Orlando
utterances.text: If I can, I'm so sorry, if we can just also interject from what we see from our perspective for veterans who are coming through our doors.

utterances.speaker: Nicole Orlando
utterances.text: So in the months from July to August of 2026, what we see is that Council District 14, 15, and 31, we see the most requests for housing assistance to our agency, just to provide some more color.

utterances.speaker: Crystal Hudson
utterances.text: For housing assistance specifically in July through August of this year.

utterances.speaker: Nicole Orlando
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: Councilmember Wong.

utterances.speaker: Crystal Hudson
utterances.text: Oh.

utterances.speaker: Crystal Hudson
utterances.text: Thank you, Jim.

utterances.speaker: Crystal Hudson
utterances.text: I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: Crystal Hudson
utterances.text: And when you said thank you, I thought you were saying hang tight.

utterances.speaker: Crystal Hudson
utterances.text: Oh, sorry.

utterances.speaker: Crystal Hudson
utterances.text: No, I'm just thanking her for the answer.

utterances.speaker: Crystal Hudson
utterances.text: Hold on.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: I know you got a birthday party to get to, but hold your horses.

chapters.summary: Hudson asks how veterans who do not initially disclose are identified; Russell says veterans self-report at intake, can disclose later, and DHS asks if they wish to identify and transfers single men to Borden if desired.
chapters.title: Hudson asks Russell how veterans are identified at intake

utterances.speaker: Crystal Hudson
utterances.text: How are veterans identified when they enter the shelter system, particularly those who do not initially disclose their military service?

utterances.speaker: Erin Dalton
utterances.text: Yeah, thank you.

utterances.speaker: Erin Dalton
utterances.text: I'm going to turn it over to the deputy commissioner to walk through that.

utterances.speaker: Sonia Russell
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Sonia Russell
utterances.text: So our veterans self-report at the point of intake.

utterances.speaker: Sonia Russell
utterances.text: So we have several intake sites, as Commissioner Adams had mentioned, for adult families, families with children and single adults.

utterances.speaker: Sonia Russell
utterances.text: So our veterans do self-report their veteran status at the intake.

utterances.speaker: Sonia Russell
utterances.text: However, if a veteran chooses not to disclose at the point of intake,

utterances.speaker: Sonia Russell
utterances.text: And however, they disclose throughout their shelter stay once they arrive to their program shelter.

utterances.speaker: Sonia Russell
utterances.text: And after meeting with their case manager or someone on staff, they share that they are a veteran.

utterances.speaker: Sonia Russell
utterances.text: We do engage and ask whether or not they wish to identify as a veteran so we can identify them in our system as such.

utterances.speaker: Sonia Russell
utterances.text: If they agree to do so, if it's a single male, then again, we will transfer that person to Borden or again, wherever shelter they wish to be placed at.

utterances.speaker: Sonia Russell
utterances.text: So we do continue to have conversations with our veterans at the point of intake and even while in shelter.

chapters.summary: Hudson asks if HUD-VASH and supportive housing are sufficient; Russell says HUD-VASH vouchers have declined, the city prioritizes veterans for CityFHEPS, and uses supportive housing and one-shot deals.
chapters.title: Hudson asks about veteran-specific housing resources

utterances.speaker: Crystal Hudson
utterances.text: Okay, and would you say there are sufficient veteran-specific housing?

utterances.speaker: Crystal Hudson
utterances.text: resources, including supportive housing and HUD-VASH vouchers to meet the current need.

utterances.speaker: Sonia Russell
utterances.text: So as Commissioner Dalton indicated, the number of HUD-VASH vouchers have declined.

utterances.speaker: Sonia Russell
utterances.text: So the resources with respect to the HUD-VASH, again, the federal government is responsible.

utterances.speaker: Sonia Russell
utterances.text: But as it relates to the city subsidies that we have, specifically City for HEPS, we do prioritize our veterans with City for HEPS.

utterances.speaker: Sonia Russell
utterances.text: So they have those vouchers.

utterances.speaker: Sonia Russell
utterances.text: We also have them complete the CAPS survey if they qualify supportive housing.

utterances.speaker: Sonia Russell
utterances.text: So between the supportive housing city, perhaps, if a veteran is over income, you know, we do assist with the enhanced one-shot deal or the SOTA program.

utterances.speaker: Sonia Russell
utterances.text: Again, these are all housing resources that we utilize to assist our veterans in moving into permanency.

utterances.speaker: Crystal Hudson
utterances.text: Thank you.

chapters.summary: Hudson asks how many veterans receive other subsidies; Dalton says of 414 subsidized placements in FY26, 41% were CityFHEPS, 26% HUD-VASH, 20% supportive housing, 5% one-shot, and 4% Section 8.
chapters.title: Hudson asks about subsidies other than HUD-VASH

utterances.speaker: Crystal Hudson
utterances.text: And do you know how many veterans are receiving housing subsidies other than HUD-VASH vouchers, such as one-shot deals or city FEPS?

utterances.speaker: Erin Dalton
utterances.text: Yeah, I can provide that for FY26 for subsidized placements.

utterances.speaker: Erin Dalton
utterances.text: So for the 414 subsidized placements during that time, 41% were city FEPS, 26% were HUD-VASH, 20% were supportive housing.

utterances.speaker: Erin Dalton
utterances.text: Another 5% were EOSD or SOTA.

utterances.speaker: Erin Dalton
utterances.text: 4% Section 8 and other, which includes NYCHA,

utterances.speaker: Crystal Hudson
utterances.text: Section 8 was, sorry, how much?

utterances.speaker: Crystal Hudson
utterances.text: Okay, thank you.

chapters.summary: Hudson asks the average time in shelter before permanent housing; Dalton gives 281 days systemwide, 285 for single adults, 199 for adult families, and 269 for families with children.
chapters.title: Hudson asks average length of stay in shelter

utterances.speaker: Crystal Hudson
utterances.text: And what is the average amount of time a veteran spends in shelter before securing permanent housing?

utterances.speaker: Erin Dalton
utterances.text: Yeah, we've got that as well.

utterances.speaker: Erin Dalton
utterances.text: Hold on one sec.

utterances.speaker: Erin Dalton
utterances.text: I prefer a different, not prefer a different number.

utterances.speaker: Erin Dalton
utterances.text: I've got a flip over here.

utterances.speaker: Erin Dalton
utterances.text: So this is data from June 5th, 2026, and I think provides the best look at length of stay.

utterances.speaker: Erin Dalton
utterances.text: So the average length of stay, and we can also get you more detail if this doesn't help, is

utterances.speaker: Erin Dalton
utterances.text: 281 days across the whole system for single adult veterans.

utterances.speaker: Erin Dalton
utterances.text: It's 285 days.

utterances.speaker: Erin Dalton
utterances.text: Adult families with veterans, 199 days.

utterances.speaker: Erin Dalton
utterances.text: Families with children with veterans, 269 days.

utterances.speaker: Crystal Hudson
utterances.text: I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: Crystal Hudson
utterances.text: Can you repeat those again?

utterances.speaker: Erin Dalton
utterances.text: Yes, I can.

utterances.speaker: Erin Dalton
utterances.text: Average across the whole system, 281 days.

utterances.speaker: Erin Dalton
utterances.text: Yep.

utterances.speaker: Erin Dalton
utterances.text: Adults, 285.

utterances.speaker: Erin Dalton
utterances.text: Adult family, 199.

utterances.speaker: Erin Dalton
utterances.text: Family with children, 269.

utterances.speaker: Crystal Hudson
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Crystal Hudson
utterances.text: I turn it back over to the chair.

utterances.speaker: Nicole Orlando
utterances.text: Councilmember Wong.

chapters.summary: Wong says the library funded by his predecessor was closed during his visit; Dalton says the library is lovely and functioning and a movie was announced there last night, while Wong says residents told a different story.
chapters.title: Wong questions Dalton on library access at Borden

utterances.speaker: Phil Wong
utterances.text: Thank you, Chair.

utterances.speaker: Phil Wong
utterances.text: My predecessor, Robert Holden, he funded the computers in the library.

utterances.speaker: Phil Wong
utterances.text: He funded the books there.

utterances.speaker: Phil Wong
utterances.text: When I visited the site with Councilmember Julie Wan, the room was closed.

utterances.speaker: Phil Wong
utterances.text: And then I spoke to the residents, why is it closed?

utterances.speaker: Phil Wong
utterances.text: Well,

utterances.speaker: Phil Wong
utterances.text: They didn't give a reason.

utterances.speaker: Phil Wong
utterances.text: So can you tell me why is it closed and they have no access to the room?

utterances.speaker: Erin Dalton
utterances.text: I can report on what I saw and what I heard last night.

utterances.speaker: Erin Dalton
utterances.text: So the library is lovely, well-functioning.

utterances.speaker: Erin Dalton
utterances.text: There's a nice table, there's some nice seated chairs, and there are books around the corners, around the walls.

utterances.speaker: Erin Dalton
utterances.text: That is the place that I held a listening session with residents, and they absolutely came in and out and used that room.

utterances.speaker: Erin Dalton
utterances.text: Also, last night, when I was with Chair Hudson on an unannounced visit, there was a, I heard over the loudspeaker, an announcement that a movie was being shown in the library.

utterances.speaker: Erin Dalton
utterances.text: And so those two things indicate.

utterances.speaker: Erin Dalton
utterances.text: to me that the library is very much functioning and in use.

utterances.speaker: Phil Wong
utterances.text: Okay, so you're telling me that residents do have access to the library as well as the materials inside?

utterances.speaker: Erin Dalton
utterances.text: That is my understanding, and my testimony is based on those two things.

utterances.speaker: Erin Dalton
utterances.text: I did find the 911 for you if you'd like it.

utterances.speaker: Phil Wong
utterances.text: All right, well...

utterances.speaker: Phil Wong
utterances.text: I was told a very different story that they have no access.

utterances.speaker: Phil Wong
utterances.text: So if I'm glad that these visits will allow these facilities to be open again, that's good news, right?

utterances.speaker: Phil Wong
utterances.text: So that's my question, Chair.

utterances.speaker: Phil Wong
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Phil Wong
utterances.text: Thank you.

chapters.summary: Morano asks the median days from request to move-in; Smalls says seven to eight months, and the longest step is obtaining documentation like birth certificates and IDs.
chapters.title: Morano asks Smalls about median time to permanent housing

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: I have a number of questions, but I want to be respectful of the members of the public that have been waiting here for two and a half hours to share their perspective on what's going on, not only with Borden Avenue, but on a lot of the legislation that we're considering today.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: But Commissioner Mata, before we wrap.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: You described an extensive process involving vouchers, apartment inspections, documentation, approvals, and multiple agencies.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: Can you tell us the median number of days between a veteran first requesting housing assistance and actually moving into permanent housing?

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: How long does the whole thing usually take?

utterances.speaker: Yesenia Mata
utterances.text: Thank you for that question.

utterances.speaker: Yesenia Mata
utterances.text: I'll pass it on to my Associate Commissioner, Donnie Smalls.

utterances.speaker: Donnie Smalls
utterances.text: Thank you for that question.

utterances.speaker: Donnie Smalls
utterances.text: The median can take anywhere between seven months to eight months for a veteran to move into permanent housing.

utterances.speaker: Donnie Smalls
utterances.text: situation or each circumstance is different depending on what this veteran has.

utterances.speaker: Donnie Smalls
utterances.text: If he has, he or she has documentation coming into shelter, if they do not have any documentation and we have to help, then that time period makes it a little bit longer.

utterances.speaker: Donnie Smalls
utterances.text: But my housing team

utterances.speaker: Donnie Smalls
utterances.text: walks through that process with them along with DHS and our community partners to get the adequate documents that they need to move into permanent housing.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: So for that seven months, which step usually takes the longest amount of time?

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: And is there anything we could do to reduce that?

utterances.speaker: Donnie Smalls
utterances.text: It can be the documents.

utterances.speaker: Donnie Smalls
utterances.text: The documentation, because most veterans could come into shelter.

utterances.speaker: Donnie Smalls
utterances.text: They might not have a birth certificate.

utterances.speaker: Donnie Smalls
utterances.text: They might not have a social security card or a photo ID.

utterances.speaker: Donnie Smalls
utterances.text: And in order to get those, you need one or the other.

utterances.speaker: Donnie Smalls
utterances.text: So that can take an extensive amount of time.

utterances.speaker: Donnie Smalls
utterances.text: I know because I've helped many veterans try to get their documents.

utterances.speaker: Donnie Smalls
utterances.text: I've also walked through the steps with them.

utterances.speaker: Donnie Smalls
utterances.text: So just getting their legalization documents can take a long time.

utterances.speaker: Donnie Smalls
utterances.text: And then once they get that, it can move a little bit faster.

utterances.speaker: Donnie Smalls
utterances.text: But then, you know, we have to go through the different agencies to move forward with housing.

chapters.summary: Morano notes 55 women veterans in shelter and asks if DSS assessed a dedicated facility for military sexual trauma; Dalton says it has not been assessed but is open to looking, and Russell says numbers have historically been low but may be revisited.
chapters.title: Morano asks Dalton about dedicated shelter for women veterans

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: Commissioner Dalton, hearing from two distinguished female veterans brings me back to your conversation earlier about women veterans in the shelter system.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: Your testimony said that.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: 55 women veterans were in shelter as of last week.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: Currently, New York City doesn't have a shelter exclusively for women veterans.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: I'm wondering if DSS has assessed whether women veterans would benefit from a dedicated facility or some sort of specialized.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: programming, particularly people that might be dealing with military sexual trauma and everything that comes with that.

utterances.speaker: Erin Dalton
utterances.text: In my time here, we have not assessed that, or at least that I'm unaware if we had.

utterances.speaker: Erin Dalton
utterances.text: But I think it's an excellent point, and we can take a look at that issue as we think about the system and system capacity going forward.

utterances.speaker: Erin Dalton
utterances.text: It's a relatively small number, but I understand the perspective for sure that...

utterances.speaker: Erin Dalton
utterances.text: That veterans and female veterans may also have special sets of circumstances and needs that could be served well in one facility.

utterances.speaker: Erin Dalton
utterances.text: We do, as we testified, have two facilities that have set aside spaces for female veterans where we do consolidate services.

utterances.speaker: Erin Dalton
utterances.text: It is run by the same provider that has veteran expertise on the single adult male side.

utterances.speaker: Erin Dalton
utterances.text: Deputy Commissioner, do you have anything to add to that?

utterances.speaker: Sonia Russell
utterances.text: So I just want to speak to historically we've always had

utterances.speaker: Sonia Russell
utterances.text: relatively low women veterans in shelter.

utterances.speaker: Sonia Russell
utterances.text: So we saw an uptick as recent as maybe 12, 18 months ago, but the number of female veterans in shelter has been between 30 or below, hence why there's never been a dedicated shelter specifically for them.

utterances.speaker: Sonia Russell
utterances.text: But as Commissioner Dalton pointed out, and as you pointed out as well, perhaps this is something that we should definitely revisit as we start to see the numbers of women coming into

utterances.speaker: Sonia Russell
utterances.text: the system.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: I would venture to guess that the number of transgender veterans is also relatively low, but that still was enough to have us opt out of $1.4 million of federal grant money.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: So even if there are only 30 or 40 or 58 female homeless veterans, if we could find facilities to make sure that they're accommodated and getting the services they need, I think that's an investment that taxpayers should certainly be interested in making.

chapters.summary: Morano asks the three most serious complaints from the Borden listening session; Dalton says food, showers, and security, and says ICL held a house meeting and is working on improvements; Morano then asks about the library portrait, and Hudson says staff identified him as someone who funded the library.
chapters.title: Morano asks Dalton about top complaints and library portrait

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: But my last question for Commissioner Dalton.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: You testified that you personally participated in a listening session with about 20 Borden Avenue residents and received mixed or negative feedback about building conditions, food, security, services, a lot of the things that you've referred to.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: What were the three most serious complaints that you heard directly most from those veterans?

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: And I'm wondering, have there been any concrete changes that have been made in response?

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: I know you mentioned the possibility of bringing in military.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: chefs to address the food issue.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: Has there been any specific changes that have already been made as a result of that listening session?

utterances.speaker: Erin Dalton
utterances.text: Yeah, thank you.

utterances.speaker: Erin Dalton
utterances.text: Thank you for the question.

utterances.speaker: Erin Dalton
utterances.text: I think the complaint we heard the most about was the issue of the food.

utterances.speaker: Erin Dalton
utterances.text: And so as I testified, we're working with ICL, thinking about what we might do with the existing

utterances.speaker: Erin Dalton
utterances.text: provider and informing meal planning and talking more with the veterans.

utterances.speaker: Erin Dalton
utterances.text: And we're looking at other options too, which I testified would include procurement that could allow us to use the commercial kitchen that is right there in front of folks.

utterances.speaker: Erin Dalton
utterances.text: And I didn't participate, but I know that the ICL leadership had a house meeting with the veterans

utterances.speaker: Erin Dalton
utterances.text: last evening and reported back some of the things that we heard and the changes that were being made.

utterances.speaker: Erin Dalton
utterances.text: I mean, it shouldn't have taken a lot of discussion to fix the shower issue, particularly if that has been raised for a long time.

utterances.speaker: Erin Dalton
utterances.text: But we are absolutely taking action on that.

utterances.speaker: Erin Dalton
utterances.text: I think that's an important step.

utterances.speaker: Erin Dalton
utterances.text: And then something that we haven't touched on all that much, but we are looking at, is just the issues around security and DHS.

utterances.speaker: Erin Dalton
utterances.text: working in partnership with IACL to ensure that we have the most up-to-date trainings, that DHS police support as necessary,

utterances.speaker: Erin Dalton
utterances.text: and so that we can ensure that there's, even though I am pleased to see all of the 911 calls down and the incidents down and complaints down, there's always more we can do to ensure that folks are safe.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: My final question is, when I visited Borden Avenue in the library, there was a portrait of somebody on the wall.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: At the time, nobody knew who that person was.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: Has anyone figured out who's on the wall of the library at Borden Avenue?

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: Library.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: No?

utterances.speaker: Nicole Orlando
utterances.text: No?

utterances.speaker: Nicole Orlando
utterances.text: No?

utterances.speaker: Crystal Hudson
utterances.text: Yes, there was.

utterances.speaker: Crystal Hudson
utterances.text: There's a staff at the facility who identified the gentleman, though I don't recall.

utterances.speaker: Crystal Hudson
utterances.text: But the gentleman has been identified.

utterances.speaker: Crystal Hudson
utterances.text: We'll be sure to report back.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: We're going to find out the identity of that person so everybody knows.

utterances.speaker: Crystal Hudson
utterances.text: He was somebody who funded...

utterances.speaker: Crystal Hudson
utterances.text: He funded the library or something like that.

utterances.speaker: Crystal Hudson
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: Commissioners, thank you very much for your testimony.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: Deputy Commissioners and Chief of Staff Orlando, certainly.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: Thank you all very, very much.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: Mm-hmm.

chapters.summary: Morano says public testimony is the most important part, outlines decorum rules and five-minute speaking limits, notes written testimony is accepted, and calls Jody Rudin, Leroy Belton, and Anne-Marie Foster.
chapters.title: Morano opens public testimony, outlines rules, and calls first panel

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: In a moment, we are going to open the hearing for public testimony.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: As far as I'm concerned, this is the absolute most important part of the hearing.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: As interested as I am in hearing from the administration, I'm much more interested in hearing from the public.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: I want to begin by...

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: thanking everybody for their patience in waiting here, whether they're waiting to testify in Zoom or especially everybody that made their way here in person.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: But a lot of my colleagues and I have a lot of questions, and we wanted to make sure we asked them, and hopefully that will inform your testimony as well.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: For anybody that can't testify, that can't stick around, feel free to submit testimony in writing as well.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: As far as, you know, Chair Hudson mentioned earlier the tradition of council members grandstanding on occasion.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: As somebody that's been accused of grandstanding more than once myself, I can promise you that I will stay and listen to.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: Every last person from the public that has made their way to testify here today, and that everybody that can't stay, that submits testimony and writing, I can promise you I'll be reviewing every single person's testimony and writing as well.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: With that...

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: I will remind members of the public that this is a formal government proceeding and that decorum shall be observed at all times.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: As such, members of the public shall remain silent at all times.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: The witness takes, see, I apologize to that gentleman for not reading that earlier.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: Sorry to him.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: The witness table is reserved for people who wish to testify.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: No video recording or photography is allowed from the witness table.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: Further, members of the public may not present audio.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: or video recordings as testimony, but may submit transcripts of such recordings to the Sergeant at Arms for inclusion in the hearing record.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: If you wish to speak at today's hearing, please fill out an appearance card with the Sergeant at Arms and wait to be recognized.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: When recognized, you will have five minutes to speak.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: A lot of other committees only give you three.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: We are giving you five to make sure you have as much time as the council members have.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: And please keep your testimony focused on today's topic, veteran homelessness in New York City, or on the legislation that we're hearing today.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: We'll hear all in-person testimony first, then turn to Zoom.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: If you have a written statement or additional written testimony you wish to submit for the record, please provide a copy of that testimony to the Sergeant at Arms.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: We'll now call the first panel.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: I want to welcome Jody Rudin, the president of ICL, Leroy Belton, a former ICL client, and Anne-Marie Foster, the president and CEO of Phoenix House.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: Please come on down, be seated, and we will get started.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: We have about five, just everybody's aware, we have about five panels from the public that are going to be testifying, which I think is great.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: I hope we get 25 panels of people coming to testify.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: I hope I'm here until midnight tonight listening to concerns, questions, thoughts, opinions from the public.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: Are we going to have Mr.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: Belton and Ms.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: Foster?

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: Great.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: Hi.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: Ms.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: Ruden, if you want to begin, please do so.

chapters.summary: Morano thanks providers for their work, acknowledges complaints but appreciates staff effort, and invites Jody Rudin to begin.
chapters.title: Morano welcomes ICL and Phoenix House panel

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: First, before you begin, actually, I'll say, you know, a lot of us who are trying to do the right thing by our veterans or people that are in shelters generally, we're quick to complain.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: And sometimes I'm concerned that that has the effect of people like you or other providers that spend a lot of time and effort trying to

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: help people that that leads those folks to feeling like their work is not appreciated.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: Know that however many complaints I have about Borden Avenue or any other facility, I really appreciate and recognize the work that not only you do, but your staff does.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: Thank you for doing it.

chapters.summary: Rudin introduces herself as ICL CEO, says the country can do better for veterans, notes the city owns the building and is funding roof and shower repairs, and says there are no leaks where residents sleep.
chapters.title: Jody Rudin testifies on ICL's role and Borden building challenges

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jody Rudin
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jody Rudin
utterances.text: Thank you to both chairs and for the committee on your leadership in holding this hearing and for shining a light on the issue.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jody Rudin
utterances.text: And I want to pick up where Chair Hudson began.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jody Rudin
utterances.text: We as a country and a city can do a lot better by the people who have served this country.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jody Rudin
utterances.text: And we bring that ethos to the work at Borden.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jody Rudin
utterances.text: proud of the work that we do, but there's always room to improve, and we try to bring a continuous quality improvement lens to the work,

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jody Rudin
utterances.text: and I too will be staying to hear what everyone has to say, all in furtherance of continuing to try to provide the best services we can.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jody Rudin
utterances.text: I thought I only had two minutes, so I'll take some liberties in elaborating as I go.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jody Rudin
utterances.text: So as you said, I'm Jody Rudin.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jody Rudin
utterances.text: I'm the CEO of ICL, and I, in partnership with DHS, am responsible for the Borden Avenue shelter, for the services and supports provided to the veterans who reside there, and for the staff members who work there.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jody Rudin
utterances.text: There are structural challenges with old buildings.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jody Rudin
utterances.text: The city owns this building and is moving ahead, as we heard, with repairs to the roof, which is causing some leaks.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jody Rudin
utterances.text: But importantly, no leaks where residents sleep.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jody Rudin
utterances.text: And they are also funding modifications to the showers to add privacy.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jody Rudin
utterances.text: And we expect to have that work completed by the end of the calendar year.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jody Rudin
utterances.text: That's the building.

chapters.summary: Rudin says Borden has 231 residents, 147 moved to permanent homes last year and 111 this year, 55% have gained or maintained employment since January 2026, overdoses are down 54%, and case managers and specialists are on staff.
chapters.title: Rudin details Borden services, placements, and employment outcomes

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jody Rudin
utterances.text: These are the services.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jody Rudin
utterances.text: We have 231 residents.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jody Rudin
utterances.text: Last year, we helped move 147 into permanent homes.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jody Rudin
utterances.text: This year, so far, 111 folks.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jody Rudin
utterances.text: A permanent home is top priority, and we exceed the city's placement targets consistently.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jody Rudin
utterances.text: Since January 2026, 55% of clients have gained or maintained employment.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jody Rudin
utterances.text: and we're supporting others in finding and securing jobs.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jody Rudin
utterances.text: Overdoses have declined by 54% compared to 2025.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jody Rudin
utterances.text: We also help veterans improve their physical and mental health, access public benefits, and partner with the city, with the federal VA, and with external organizations to deliver a host of services and programs.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jody Rudin
utterances.text: I want to say that when clients arrive, when veterans arrive at Borden, they're assigned a case manager, and we work with them on all of their goals, including to achieve permanent housing.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jody Rudin
utterances.text: And the average length of stay at Borden is around eight months.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jody Rudin
utterances.text: We have housing specialists who do this work.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jody Rudin
utterances.text: We have employment specialists who support clients in getting employment.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jody Rudin
utterances.text: We have case acts and substance use specialists who work with clients on their substance use disorders.
