utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jody Rudin
utterances.text: We also have OASIS, a state-licensed alcohol and substance use clinic

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jody Rudin
utterances.text: off-site, and we frequently bring those staff, including peers with lived experience, on-site to Borden to support people with their substance use disorders.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jody Rudin
utterances.text: We organizationally abide by an ethos of walk alone, go faster, walk together, go farther.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jody Rudin
utterances.text: I think Borden is a good example of different groups, both in and out of government, coming together to be additive.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jody Rudin
utterances.text: We get tremendous support from the city's Department of Social Services, from the city's Department of Veteran Services, from other veteran services organizations throughout the city.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jody Rudin
utterances.text: And our results are additive to one another.

chapters.summary: Rudin says Borden is a 24-7 operation, 80% of clients report a positive experience, food is the biggest complaint, the vendor changed to Healthy Beets, monthly surveys are conducted, and more changes are being explored.
chapters.title: Rudin describes resident feedback and food improvements

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jody Rudin
utterances.text: Borden is a 24-7 operation.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jody Rudin
utterances.text: It does more than provide shelter.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jody Rudin
utterances.text: It helps veterans to recover, build stability.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jody Rudin
utterances.text: Our 75 staff members work not just to provide a bed and meals, but also all the services veterans need to live dignified lives.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jody Rudin
utterances.text: We make a point of listening to our residents.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jody Rudin
utterances.text: We create opportunities for residents to provide input through biweekly meetings, community forums, surveys.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jody Rudin
utterances.text: 80% of the clients at Borden tell us that they're having a positive experience there.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jody Rudin
utterances.text: We also hear a lot of constructive feedback, and we try to act to fix things that are problematic.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jody Rudin
utterances.text: You know, we've talked a lot about food, and that is the single biggest complaint that we hear when we get together with the residents of Borden.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jody Rudin
utterances.text: We have been trying to iterate to get to a good place with food.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jody Rudin
utterances.text: A couple of years ago, we changed our food vendor from Regina to Healthy Hearts, and we prevailed upon the city to increase our food per diem.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jody Rudin
utterances.text: In the immediate aftermath of those changes, we did get good feedback from veterans.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jody Rudin
utterances.text: Now we're hearing more constructive feedback about the food.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jody Rudin
utterances.text: People have new concerns.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jody Rudin
utterances.text: So we're exploring additional changes.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jody Rudin
utterances.text: We have a monthly surveying process on food.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jody Rudin
utterances.text: We ask the vendor to throw out meals that are not popular.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jody Rudin
utterances.text: We do the more popular meals more often.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jody Rudin
utterances.text: And as the commissioner of DSS mentioned, we are in a broader strategy.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jody Rudin
utterances.text: contemplation about improving food more broadly.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jody Rudin
utterances.text: I want to say there's always room for improvement.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jody Rudin
utterances.text: Sometimes that requires more funding.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jody Rudin
utterances.text: I want to shine a light on the people who work at Borden.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jody Rudin
utterances.text: I'm really grateful to our 75 staff who show up in hazardous weather, in global pandemics, in power outages.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jody Rudin
utterances.text: They show up to serve our veterans and to do the best work they can.

chapters.summary: Rudin says bathroom privacy is not an issue, urine containers relate to medical conditions, food is not confiscated, and the culinary program has 20 slots and prioritizes Borden veterans, though no Borden clients are in the current cohort.
chapters.title: Rudin clarifies urine containers, food policy, and culinary program

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jody Rudin
utterances.text: I absolutely need to clarify the urine in people's living spaces.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jody Rudin
utterances.text: There is, first of all, let it be very clear, privacy in the bathroom, stalls with doors that can be closed.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jody Rudin
utterances.text: Privacy is not an issue in the bathrooms.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jody Rudin
utterances.text: It's not something we've historically heard feedback on.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jody Rudin
utterances.text: When people are urinating in containers, it relates to a specific medical condition.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jody Rudin
utterances.text: And so that's a set of exceptions for people who have medical concerns.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jody Rudin
utterances.text: And of course, we encourage folks to clean out those containers so that we can provide a clean and habitable shelter.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jody Rudin
utterances.text: I also want to make clear that food is not confiscated.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jody Rudin
utterances.text: We have an area, a room where people can bring food and eat from the outside.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jody Rudin
utterances.text: We have recently learned from DSS that people can bring food from the outside and eat it in the cafeteria.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jody Rudin
utterances.text: So we are in the process of creating a process for that.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jody Rudin
utterances.text: I also lastly want to be clear that the culinary arts training program that we have on site with Project Renewal has capacity for 20 people.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jody Rudin
utterances.text: cohort, it would make us thrilled if all 20 were clients at Borden.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jody Rudin
utterances.text: Last cycle, we had no clients from Borden.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jody Rudin
utterances.text: Now, this bespeaks the fact that we have a high employment rate, and this is a rigorous food training program, but we are always interested in prioritizing clients,

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jody Rudin
utterances.text: residents who live at Borden, the veterans, and would do backflips to do so, and would want to talk to you, Councilmember Wong, offline, if you've heard from people who aren't getting access to the program.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jody Rudin
utterances.text: One thing that comes to mind is it's possible that they expressed interest after the cohort begins, so we would need to wait for the new cohort, but they are always welcome.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jody Rudin
utterances.text: That is our priority, and candidly, one of our reasons why we wanted to host this program at the Borden Avenue residence.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jody Rudin
utterances.text: Thank you all for your time.

chapters.summary: Morano asks about leaks and tarps; Rudin says the city owns the building, seven units are offline, the number fluctuates with rainfall, and the city patches the roof.
chapters.title: Morano questions Rudin on leaks and offline beds

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: I have a couple of minor questions, brief questions, I should say.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: Just on the...

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: Because it was the most glaring issue I observed when I was there, the leaking and the tarps.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: Commissioner Dalton indicated that there were about seven beds that were offline as a result of the leaks.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: Is that the case?

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: And is that the case even when there's heavy rains and things like that?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jody Rudin
utterances.text: Yeah, I mean, it's important for me to clarify that the city owns the building and is responsible for the repairs in the capital.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jody Rudin
utterances.text: Yeah, the city is in regular touch with us before and after each rainfall to figure out the direction that the rain is leaking into the facility.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jody Rudin
utterances.text: We can iterate a process around making sure that beds are offline so that people aren't impacted by the rain.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jody Rudin
utterances.text: Currently, we have seven units offline.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jody Rudin
utterances.text: It's possible that that could fluctuate based on the direction of the rainfall and, most importantly, based on the remediation work that the city is doing to patch the roof.

chapters.summary: Morano asks about 231 capacity versus 168 residents; Rudin clarifies capacity is 231 and current census is south of 200; Morano asks about long-stayers, and Rudin says factors include restrictions and complex needs, with an average stay of eight months.
chapters.title: Morano questions Rudin on capacity and long-staying residents

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: In your testimony, you said that there's 231 residents.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: We've been operating under 168 resident assumption.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: Are there more residents?

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: Yeah, let me clarify that.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jody Rudin
utterances.text: The capacity is for 231 people right now.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jody Rudin
utterances.text: We are currently south of 200.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: Got it.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: You talked about 147 veterans who moved into permanent housing last year and 111 so far this year.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: That's really encouraging, and I commend your staff.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: I'd also like to hear about the veterans who haven't been successfully housed.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: How many current residents have been at Borden Avenue for more than a year?

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: How many for more than two years?

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: And what's the longest anyone's been there?

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: For the long-staying veterans, also, what's the single biggest obstacle from getting them into permanent housing?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jody Rudin
utterances.text: I don't have the data you're asking for with respect to the longest staying resident and those who have been here for.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jody Rudin
utterances.text: Yes, absolutely.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jody Rudin
utterances.text: Listen, there are a variety of factors that could keep someone in shelter for longer than they want to be.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jody Rudin
utterances.text: Some are restrictions with respect to where they can live based on sex offense or other status.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jody Rudin
utterances.text: Some are, you know, we work with clients who have complex behavioral health needs and profiles.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jody Rudin
utterances.text: So sometimes we're working with people over time in more foundational ways to, you know.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jody Rudin
utterances.text: Help them advance their goals around treatment, help them secure the documentation they need to move into housing.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jody Rudin
utterances.text: So it can be an elaborate process, but on average, people move out in eight months.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: Got it.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: Chair Hudson.

chapters.summary: Hudson asks when ICL took over (2008) and when roof and shower issues were reported; Rudin says these have been ongoing conversations for years, and the funding amount and timeline were only known in recent weeks.
chapters.title: Hudson questions Rudin on ICL contract and repair notifications

utterances.speaker: Crystal Hudson
utterances.text: Thank you so much.

utterances.speaker: Crystal Hudson
utterances.text: Just a couple of questions as well.

utterances.speaker: Crystal Hudson
utterances.text: And apologies if you already mentioned this, but when did ICL take over the contract at Borden Avenue?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jody Rudin
Crystal Hudson
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: Crystal Hudson
utterances.text: And when did you first notify DHS or DSS of the roof issues?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jody Rudin
utterances.text: I don't have a date to give you, but we have been in an ongoing protracted discussion over the course of many years with the city about the roof.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jody Rudin
utterances.text: And they informed us some number of years ago that it was in the city's capital plan.

utterances.speaker: Crystal Hudson
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: Crystal Hudson
utterances.text: Would you say it dates back to 2008?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jody Rudin
utterances.text: I would be hard-pressed to say that, but it has certainly been an ongoing topic for many, many, many years.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jody Rudin
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jody Rudin
utterances.text: It may well have dated back that far.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jody Rudin
utterances.text: I just don't know.

utterances.speaker: Crystal Hudson
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: Crystal Hudson
utterances.text: That's fair.

utterances.speaker: Crystal Hudson
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Crystal Hudson
utterances.text: And then when did ICL first notify DHS or DSS regarding concerns with the shower facilities and privacy conditions?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jody Rudin
utterances.text: Yes, similarly, this has been an ongoing conversation over an extended period.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jody Rudin
utterances.text: We, as you can imagine, we're, you know, DHS is our partner and our collaborator.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jody Rudin
utterances.text: And we also, one feature of our relationship, and this is not unique to ICL and Borden, it's the case across our portfolio of shelters.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jody Rudin
utterances.text: I imagine my colleagues would say it's the case for them.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jody Rudin
utterances.text: Advocating, raising challenges and advocating for more resources for the people we serve is a permanent feature of our relationship.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jody Rudin
utterances.text: So in both the case of the showers and the roof, these have been ongoing conversations that have played out over time.

utterances.speaker: Crystal Hudson
utterances.text: And when were you notified of that the funding was secured for both the roof?

utterances.speaker: Crystal Hudson
utterances.text: And shower improvements.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jody Rudin
utterances.text: We had been notified in the last couple of years that the roof was in the capital plan.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jody Rudin
utterances.text: We did not know the funding amount and we did not know the timeframe until the last many weeks.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jody Rudin
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jody Rudin
utterances.text: And the showers too, our new need was approved to hire the vendor in the last couple of weeks.

utterances.speaker: Crystal Hudson
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: Crystal Hudson
utterances.text: And, um,

chapters.summary: Hudson asks what repairs ICL can authorize without DHS approval; Rudin says physical plant issues go to DHS, superficial things like painting may be in ICL's purview, and even shower curtain rods required a DHS process.

utterances.text: Sorry, I have one last question.

utterances.speaker: Crystal Hudson
utterances.text: What categories of repairs or facility improvements can ICL authorize and complete independently without prior DHS or DSS approval?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jody Rudin
utterances.text: But they intercede.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jody Rudin
utterances.text: They have capital experts that we don't.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jody Rudin

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: Thank you, Chair.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: Ms.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: Foster.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: I didn't realize I wasn't told you had a question.

chapters.summary: Wong asks about library and computer access; Rudin says the library is open 24-7 and flyers will be posted; Wong asks why the culinary school can use the kitchen but veterans cannot, and Rudin says there is no cap on veterans and the commercial kitchen is not for resident cooking.
chapters.title: Wong questions Rudin on library, computers, and culinary school

utterances.speaker: Phil Wong
utterances.text: Three questions, yeah.

utterances.speaker: Phil Wong
utterances.text: Miss Jody Rudin?

utterances.speaker: Phil Wong
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: Phil Wong
utterances.text: You're based out of 125 Broad Street.

utterances.speaker: Phil Wong
utterances.text: Is that right?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jody Rudin
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: Phil Wong
utterances.text: How often do you visit the Borden Avenue facility?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jody Rudin
utterances.text: Multiple times a year.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jody Rudin
utterances.text: It depends.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jody Rudin
utterances.text: Some years I've been there a dozen times.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jody Rudin
utterances.text: Some years fewer times.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jody Rudin
utterances.text: It varies.

utterances.speaker: Phil Wong
utterances.text: When was your last visit?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jody Rudin
utterances.text: Last night.

utterances.speaker: Phil Wong
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: Phil Wong
utterances.text: Okay, so I have two questions.

utterances.speaker: Phil Wong
utterances.text: Can, like, when I was there with Council Member Julie Wan,

utterances.speaker: Phil Wong
utterances.text: There were residents there who told me they have no access to the computers and no access to the library.

utterances.speaker: Phil Wong
utterances.text: And there's a gentleman that walked out a couple minutes ago before you testified that they still have no access to the computers.

utterances.speaker: Phil Wong
utterances.text: Now, is my understanding that...

utterances.speaker: Phil Wong
utterances.text: The part of the contract is to have computers there so veterans could use them.

utterances.speaker: Phil Wong
utterances.text: So can you tell me why that they cannot, they have no access?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jody Rudin
utterances.text: Absolutely.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jody Rudin
utterances.text: And I appreciate your question.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jody Rudin
utterances.text: And we enjoyed what I think was an enormously productive relationship with Councilmember Holden.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jody Rudin
utterances.text: And we are ever grateful for his investments in the facility, including at the library.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jody Rudin
utterances.text: The library is open on a 24-7 basis.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jody Rudin
utterances.text: There may be some specific exceptions to that if there's a meeting or if we're hosting visitors.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jody Rudin
utterances.text: But in the ordinary course of business, it's open on a 24-7 basis.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jody Rudin
utterances.text: There have been a few things that you've said or that I've heard on the panel that just aren't true.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jody Rudin
utterances.text: And I would welcome a relationship where you're bringing those issues to us.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jody Rudin
utterances.text: We can figure out the source of the disagreement or misunderstanding and fix it immediately.

utterances.speaker: Phil Wong
utterances.text: So the residents now have free access to the library and the computers.

utterances.speaker: Phil Wong
utterances.text: Is that right?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jody Rudin
utterances.text: Yeah, absolutely.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jody Rudin
utterances.text: And hearing that this has been a source of misunderstanding, we'll post flyers just to clarify the hours.

utterances.speaker: Phil Wong
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: Phil Wong
utterances.text: Finally, I raised the question before.

utterances.speaker: Phil Wong
utterances.text: Could you answer?

utterances.speaker: Phil Wong
utterances.text: How come the culinary schools could use the cooking facilities there but not the veterans?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jody Rudin
utterances.text: Yeah, thank you.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jody Rudin
utterances.text: This was another point I wanted to clarify, so I'm grateful for the question.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jody Rudin
utterances.text: So the culinary arts training program has cohorts of 20 people at a given time.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jody Rudin
utterances.text: That number is determined based on the size of the kitchen and how many people can comfortably fit.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jody Rudin
utterances.text: There is no cap on the number of veterans who can participate from Borden.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jody Rudin
utterances.text: If we had our druthers, all 20 would participate from Borden.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jody Rudin
utterances.text: In this current cycle, we don't have any veterans from Borden in the cohort.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jody Rudin
utterances.text: So we would love your support in drumming up interest.

utterances.speaker: Phil Wong
utterances.text: Now, my question was.

utterances.speaker: Phil Wong
utterances.text: When they say their cooking classes are not in session, how come the veterans have no access to the facility to cook their own food or eat or to heat up their own food because they are hungry?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jody Rudin
utterances.text: Yeah, so I think actually both Chair Hudson and our colleague from DSS, Sonia Russell, clarified it is not customary for people who live in shelters to access the commercial kitchen for their cooking use.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jody Rudin
utterances.text: It is incumbent upon us to provide them.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jody Rudin
utterances.text: three meals a day, consistent with the New York City food and nutrition standards.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jody Rudin
utterances.text: So I've never heard of a scenario where people living in the residence would access the commercial kitchen.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jody Rudin
utterances.text: Now, we have heard feedback on, can we have an air fryer?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jody Rudin
utterances.text: Can we have more microwaves?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jody Rudin
utterances.text: And that is something that we're working on bringing into the cafeteria so that people can have more autonomy around bringing in food, heating up food.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jody Rudin
utterances.text: But it's not traditional practice to let people gain access to the commercial kitchen where there's all sorts of mechanicals that they may or may not know how to use and would introduce, I think, health and safety concerns.

utterances.speaker: Phil Wong
utterances.text: Okay, thank you.

utterances.speaker: Phil Wong
utterances.text: I'll be in touch.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jody Rudin
utterances.text: Yeah, I genuinely look forward to it.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jody Rudin
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Phil Wong
utterances.text: Thank you, Chair.

utterances.speaker: Phil Wong
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Crystal Hudson
utterances.text: Ms.

utterances.speaker: Crystal Hudson
utterances.text: Foster, thank you for your patience.

chapters.summary: Foster introduces herself as Phoenix House CEO, describes veteran-specific residential and outpatient programs, collaboration with Borden, and says housing alone is not enough without behavioral health treatment.
chapters.title: Anne-Marie Foster testifies on Phoenix House veteran programs

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Anne-Marie Foster
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Chair Hudson and Chair Moreno and members of the General Welfare and Veterans Affairs Committee.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Anne-Marie Foster
utterances.text: My name is Anne-Marie Foster.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Anne-Marie Foster
utterances.text: I'm the President and CEO of Phoenix House of New York in Long Island, and I'm here to testify about the importance of veteran-specific programs and our collaboration with the Board and Avenue Shelter.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Anne-Marie Foster
utterances.text: Phoenix House has been around since 1967.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Anne-Marie Foster
utterances.text: We help New Yorkers.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Anne-Marie Foster
utterances.text: We have helped thousands of New Yorkers, people who struggle with substance use, individuals who are veterans, and they alcohol abuse, and we help them lead healthy and what we call rewarding lives.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Anne-Marie Foster
utterances.text: Phoenix House also runs residential programs.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Anne-Marie Foster
utterances.text: specifically for veterans.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Anne-Marie Foster
utterances.text: It is located outside of the city, but there are several other agencies that do the same for residential and outpatient specifically for veterans.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Anne-Marie Foster
utterances.text: Right now, as been said previously, New York City is currently spending millions on services for homeless

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Anne-Marie Foster
utterances.text: community members, and even as more New Yorkers are sleeping on the streets than ever before, that figure includes about 625 homeless veterans.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Anne-Marie Foster
utterances.text: Behavioral health challenges touch New Yorkers across every housing status, but state estimates suggest that up to 10% of residents experiencing homelessness also live with a substance use disorder and severe mental illness.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Anne-Marie Foster
utterances.text: And for veterans who may also carry the effects of service-related trauma, those needs can be especially acute.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Anne-Marie Foster
utterances.text: Housing is essential, but for many veterans, it is not enough on its own.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Anne-Marie Foster
utterances.text: Without treatment for the conditions that often accompany or contribute to homelessness, people struggle to stabilize, keep their housing, and move forward.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Anne-Marie Foster
utterances.text: Too often, the pathways between shelter, outreach,

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Anne-Marie Foster
utterances.text: Veteran services and behavioral health programs are fragmented.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Anne-Marie Foster
utterances.text: And a veteran who is ready for care can wait too long or fall through the cracks between systems.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Anne-Marie Foster
utterances.text: That is why veteran-specific care matters, and that is what we see when we work with the clients that come from Borden Avenue.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Anne-Marie Foster
utterances.text: We work with ICL's team to provide residents.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Anne-Marie Foster
utterances.text: at Borden with holistic programming focused on the unique needs of veterans seeking treatment.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Anne-Marie Foster
utterances.text: We have a specialized team of experts and medical staff dedicated to providing trauma-focused treatment, including individual counseling, group counseling, social and recreational activities, and skill development.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Anne-Marie Foster
utterances.text: These services are located at our Long Island City Outpatient Residential Program, and our experience shows that programs designed specifically for veterans work the best.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Anne-Marie Foster
utterances.text: We are both able to deliver services to our veterans because of support from the state.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Anne-Marie Foster
utterances.text: We are contracted through State OASIS and city investment dollars from like our opioid settlement partners and federal dollars from our SOAR grants.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Anne-Marie Foster
utterances.text: And these events, investments, the city makes and board and are critical for the success of the people who reside there.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Anne-Marie Foster
utterances.text: Again, we said it before, our veterans put their lives on the line to protect us.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Anne-Marie Foster
utterances.text: We owe it to them to do our best to support them in their recovery and the work that is happening.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Anne-Marie Foster
utterances.text: At Phoenix House and partnering with agencies like Borden can help connect our veterans to the services that they need.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Anne-Marie Foster
utterances.text: So thank you for considering my testimony.

chapters.title: Robert Pauls testifies on VA funding and FOIA delays

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Robert Pauls

utterances.text: My name is Robert Pauls.

utterances.text: I am an independent veterans advocate.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Robert Pauls

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Robert Pauls
utterances.text: Neither are willing to provide any report regarding the reduction of funding of the BAVR except through FOIA, which is currently not available.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Robert Pauls
utterances.text: My information is that the information from either office will not be available until December.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Robert Pauls
utterances.text: The other issue that I had was New York City.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Robert Pauls
utterances.text: DHS not having a dedicated residence for women's issue, which is a minor issue here, but it's been a large one.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Robert Pauls
utterances.text: On August the 24th, I distributed an introductory proposal.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Robert Pauls
utterances.text: Again, not having the information which I've received here today with regard to DHS and also DVS and DSS

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Robert Pauls
utterances.text: documentation provided today, I will refrain.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Robert Pauls
utterances.text: from presenting that until I have some specific statistical and actual reports, particularly the legal aspects of

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Robert Pauls
utterances.text: the access to Borden Avenue by the

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Robert Pauls
utterances.text: Council of New York, as well as VSOs and other issues, because that has been a major problem.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Robert Pauls
utterances.text: I'd like to thank everyone.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Robert Pauls
utterances.text: Bye-bye.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: Thank you, sir.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: Yep, go ahead.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: We'll go boop, boop, boop, boop.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: Yep.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: Close to the mic, if you would.

chapters.summary: Silas thanks DVS staff, says he was displaced in November 2025 and had his own apartment by June, received PTSD services at James J. Peters Hospital, and is grateful for the help.
chapters.title: Rodney Silas testifies on successful housing transition

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Rodney Silas
utterances.text: There you go.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Rodney Silas
utterances.text: Good afternoon, ladies and gentlemen.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Rodney Silas
utterances.text: My name is Rodney Silas.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Rodney Silas
utterances.text: I'm going to start with all praises due to Allah.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Rodney Silas
utterances.text: First of all, I'd like to thank Dr.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Rodney Silas
utterances.text: Cleopatra Brown, Donnie Smalls, Denise Covington, and Mr.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Rodney Silas
utterances.text: Fowler.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Rodney Silas
utterances.text: I was displaced November 2025.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Rodney Silas
utterances.text: By June of this year, I have my own apartment now, and I'm grateful.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Rodney Silas
utterances.text: I went there.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Rodney Silas
utterances.text: I handled my business.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Rodney Silas
utterances.text: And they took very good care of me.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Rodney Silas
utterances.text: Now, I also received services from James J.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Rodney Silas
utterances.text: Peters Hospital for PTSD.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Rodney Silas
utterances.text: And a military-related injury.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Rodney Silas
utterances.text: My process, I handled my business, and they went beyond the call of duty to help me, and I'm grateful.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Rodney Silas
utterances.text: You know, I really don't have much to say because I get emotional.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Rodney Silas
utterances.text: You know, because...

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Rodney Silas
utterances.text: I've never been in a situation like this.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Rodney Silas
utterances.text: So I thank all of y'all.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Rodney Silas
utterances.text: That's all I have to say.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Rodney Silas
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Crystal Hudson
utterances.text: Thank you for sharing.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: Go ahead, sir.

chapters.summary: Warner says he was technically homeless living with his parents, became a security guard at a migrant shelter and then lived in a veteran shelter, says no caseworker asked about his plan, and describes rude treatment and systemic issues.
chapters.title: Charles Warner describes homelessness and caseworker problems

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Charles Warner
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Charles Warner
utterances.text: My name is Charles Warner.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Charles Warner
utterances.text: I'm a Navy vet who was honorably discharged in May 2000.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Charles Warner
utterances.text: I came back home to New York City to deal with family issues as I became unemployed in another state.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Charles Warner
utterances.text: When I came back to New York, I immediately looked into the process of how to get my own place, get established on my own feet.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Charles Warner
utterances.text: And what I've come to find out is that I was already homeless the entire time I was living in New York because I didn't have a place of my own.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Charles Warner
utterances.text: According to regulations or laws or whatever the stipulations were,

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Charles Warner
utterances.text: the requirement to get services to become a housed veteran means that you have to be documented.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Charles Warner
utterances.text: As not having a residence of your own.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Charles Warner
utterances.text: You have to be documented of being on the street or being in a shelter.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Charles Warner
utterances.text: I came back here in February 2009, and I was living in my parents'home from February 2009 to my father's death.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Charles Warner
utterances.text: Three years ago.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Charles Warner
utterances.text: Because of that, I was technically homeless, but I was still in a house because an unattainable of getting services because I had a roof over my head.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Charles Warner
utterances.text: But I was still homeless.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Charles Warner
utterances.text: So I actually had to go into...

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Charles Warner
utterances.text: Dire situations where I ended up getting evicted from that residence because the income I was guaranteeing from my job as a security guard,

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Charles Warner
utterances.text: by the way, at homeless shelters for veterans, I mean, at homeless shelters for migrants.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Charles Warner
utterances.text: OK, that I couldn't afford my own place, that I ended up going from working as a security guard in a shelter for migrants

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Charles Warner
utterances.text: to live in my own shelter as a veteran.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Charles Warner
utterances.text: That's an oxymoron.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Charles Warner
utterances.text: And then every time I spoke to a person at ICL about my plan to get out of the shelter system,

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Charles Warner
utterances.text: There was not a single person interested in what my plan was.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Charles Warner
utterances.text: No one in the entire time I was there from August to April.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Charles Warner
utterances.text: Ask me what my plan actually was.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Charles Warner
utterances.text: My initial caseworker was...

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Charles Warner
utterances.text: Was no longer working there just a week into the time of helping me.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Charles Warner
utterances.text: For whatever reason, his employment there was terminated.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Charles Warner
utterances.text: And he was replaced, and I was added to the itinerary of another caseworker who was...

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Charles Warner
utterances.text: Frankly was blatantly rude to me right from the start.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Charles Warner
utterances.text: Because what Miss Berry did is that she apparently was looking all over the shelter for me, unaware that I had a job that was not earning enough money as security.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Charles Warner
utterances.text: I was also just started back as a part-time student to complete my bachelor's degree.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Charles Warner
utterances.text: And at the same time, I was also independently looking for a place to live.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Charles Warner
utterances.text: And she was expecting me to stay in the shelter.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Charles Warner
utterances.text: Waiting for whatever services, because she said she was looking all over for me.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Charles Warner
utterances.text: Mind you, I had a cell phone that was in service, and I also had email, and they had all of this contact information, but she could not find me because she didn't see me in my cubicle.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Charles Warner
utterances.text: Also, she made it blatantly.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Charles Warner
utterances.text: clear whenever she had an issue with me to go public with it because she will have these conversations with me right there at the security entrance.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Charles Warner
utterances.text: But when I'm in the back in her office and speaking up about these issues,

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Charles Warner
utterances.text: I need to quiet down because people might hear.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Charles Warner
utterances.text: But she's going to be blatant and obvious right there in the doorway with me.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Charles Warner
utterances.text: Also, the last time I dealt with her, she actually had called one of our colleagues over into my rooming area.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Charles Warner
utterances.text: And as a witness, as if I'm going to get hostile.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Charles Warner
utterances.text: But she's the one causing the hostility.

chapters.summary: Morano thanks Warner and asks if his experience was one or two bad caseworkers or systemic; Warner says it is systemic due to overstressed staff and unwillingness to hear individual situations, and confirms he is now in permanent housing.
chapters.title: Morano asks Warner if problems are systemic

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: Mr.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: Warner, one, thank you for your service to the country.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: Second, thank you for being here today.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: I appreciate you waiting a couple hours to testify and share your perspective.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: And I know how difficult it is to hold down a job and look for housing simultaneously.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: And to do that while you're in the circumstances of being in the shelter, I can only imagine how challenging that that must have been for you.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: And I appreciate you sharing that perspective.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: Without further mentioning one specific caseworker, I'm wondering if you can speak to how you made it out of the shelter system in general and if what you experienced is...

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: is a result of one or two bad caseworkers, or if it's a systemic problem with ICL and something that they can improve upon.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: Because obviously it doesn't do you any good if you're on the receiving end of a poor caseworker, but I'm wondering if there's a systemic problem that we can try to fix to make sure others aren't in the same position that you were.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Charles Warner
utterances.text: Good question.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Charles Warner
utterances.text: It is systemic because in part you got people that are overstressed from being too much of having too much of a caseload.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Charles Warner
utterances.text: Another thing is you don't have people there that are open minded to hearing your situation.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Charles Warner
utterances.text: This panel has spoken about.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Charles Warner
utterances.text: About us being veterans and our individual situations being different.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Charles Warner
utterances.text: But they want to hear specific things that they don't, they're not willing to hear the specific needs of the individual.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Charles Warner
utterances.text: They want to collectively

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Charles Warner
utterances.text: umbrella us all together in one scenario.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Charles Warner
utterances.text: I actually have a specific scenario of how I got into this situation that I was in.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Charles Warner
utterances.text: Same as the gentleman that was right beside me.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Charles Warner
utterances.text: He had, but we're clumped together in the same scenario when it comes to receiving services.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: You're in permanent housing now?

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: Thank goodness.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: Let's stay in touch.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: I'd love to stay in touch even offline after the hearing ends.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: Grab a microphone and please identify yourself and get started when you're ready.

chapters.summary: Weth says Borden is not a residence but a holding or detention facility, says management failures run from the top down, staff are unsupervised, and there is no accountability.
chapters.title: Matt Weth calls Borden a detention facility with systemic failures

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Matt Weth
utterances.text: My name is Matt Weth.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Matt Weth
utterances.text: I was honorably discharged from the Air Force 2005.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Matt Weth
utterances.text: I had the unfortunate fortune of ending up at the Borden Avenue, as they call it, Veterans Residence, which I'd like to start right there.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Matt Weth
utterances.text: That's an open insult.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Matt Weth
utterances.text: The name of the facility, it's not a residence.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Matt Weth
utterances.text: At best, it's a holding facility.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Matt Weth
utterances.text: If I'm being honest about it, it feels much more like a detention facility.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Matt Weth
utterances.text: You asked my fellow veteran over here whether it was a couple issues or systemic.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Matt Weth
utterances.text: I like that I can look at Jody Rudin while I say this.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Matt Weth
utterances.text: It's decidedly systemic.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Matt Weth
utterances.text: Your organization's idea of what constitutes organizational management is an embarrassment to the concept itself.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Matt Weth
utterances.text: The problem is from the top down, and it's just rot exposed at every level.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Matt Weth
utterances.text: I have management experience, unfortunately for me, because I can see glaringly.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Matt Weth
utterances.text: You say lack of oversight?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Matt Weth
utterances.text: Like, yeah, lack of oversight at every level.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Matt Weth
utterances.text: The, the, uh,

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Matt Weth
utterances.text: lowest ranked employees there, if you will.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Matt Weth
utterances.text: The bulk of the staff effectively operates with no supervision.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Matt Weth
utterances.text: I couldn't tell you what their duties are supposed to be.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Matt Weth
utterances.text: Collectively, they use their numbers to abscond from responsibility.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Matt Weth
utterances.text: I can tell you if you walked in that facility right now, you wouldn't have to even be able to get in.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Matt Weth
utterances.text: If you just went in those double glass doors and looked, because you can see the desk, you know from experience, Councilperson Murano, you can see what's going on.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Matt Weth
utterances.text: In front of the, you know, beyond the double glass doors.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Matt Weth
utterances.text: I can guarantee you there are at least three or four people sitting in that office behind the desk, socializing, doing nothing.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Matt Weth
utterances.text: And they're probably all supposed to be doing something.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Matt Weth
utterances.text: And there's no management.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Matt Weth
utterances.text: Nobody is watching them or holding them accountable.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Matt Weth
utterances.text: At any level for their lack of doing anything.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Matt Weth
utterances.text: And it's a complete embarrassment.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Matt Weth
utterances.text: It's a nightmare from top to bottom in an organizational sense that I was there last week at Julie Wan's attempt.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Matt Weth
utterances.text: I saw Councilperson Wong there as well.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Matt Weth
utterances.text: Julie Wan's pitiful attempt to enter the facility.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Matt Weth
utterances.text: I say pitiful attempt because

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Matt Weth
utterances.text: From what I can gather, it was her first attempt since she took office.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Matt Weth
utterances.text: I'm a veteran.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Matt Weth
utterances.text: If I'm showing up somewhere that I'm not 100% sure I can just walk right in, I'm going to test that out beforehand so as not to avoid the embarrassment that she walked right into.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Matt Weth
utterances.text: That was really embarrassing, frankly.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Matt Weth
utterances.text: Uh,

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Matt Weth
utterances.text: That you guys can't just get it together and get her in there whenever she needs to says a lot.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Matt Weth
utterances.text: How's that?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Matt Weth
utterances.text: I'll let that one speak for itself and let everyone else draw their own conclusions.

chapters.summary: Weth says there are no windows, rooms are nine by six feet, noise echoes, he had six months of sleep deprivation, says a lawsuit is forthcoming, and recommends a paid veteran staff member to report to the council and public.
chapters.title: Weth describes inhumane conditions and sleep deprivation

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Matt Weth
utterances.text: It's a nightmare.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Matt Weth
utterances.text: You want to hear about the conditions inside the facility, outside of the obvious ones that we all harp on, like the leaky roof and the kitchen?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Matt Weth
utterances.text: Yeah, we've thoroughly beaten those horses and those need to be addressed.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Matt Weth
utterances.text: How about the fact there are no windows in the facility?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Matt Weth
utterances.text: It's a residence, right?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Matt Weth
utterances.text: Oh, there are windows that run around the top of the outside.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Matt Weth
utterances.text: That's not, it's not a living space.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Matt Weth
utterances.text: It's a warehouse or it was a manufacturing facility.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Matt Weth
utterances.text: Poorly repurposed.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Matt Weth
utterances.text: Those cells, that's a room for a human to live in?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Matt Weth
utterances.text: Are you kidding me?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Matt Weth
utterances.text: Nine by six?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Matt Weth
utterances.text: Yeah, Julie Wan did talk to me outside the facility and she, uh...

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Matt Weth
utterances.text: Used some of the information that she gleaned from our conversation when she spoke to the press.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Matt Weth
utterances.text: She brought up the fact that ourselves were smaller than is allowable by law for New York State prisons.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Matt Weth
utterances.text: Oh yeah, she just pulled that out of nowhere.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Matt Weth
utterances.text: She took that from me.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Matt Weth
utterances.text: I gave her the numbers, nine by six.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Matt Weth
utterances.text: Great.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Matt Weth
utterances.text: She got a soundbite.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Matt Weth
utterances.text: She also used the term Dickensian to describe the conditions.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Matt Weth
utterances.text: To anyone who's not culturally up to speed,

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Matt Weth
utterances.text: That's a reference to The Wire, season five.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Matt Weth
utterances.text: Scott Templeton, the lying reporter who fabricates a story to add to his own largesse, uses the term Dickensian when he's selling the story to his editor.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Matt Weth
utterances.text: His editor fawns over the term.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Matt Weth
utterances.text: Oh, yes, emphasizes the Dickensian aspect.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Matt Weth
utterances.text: Now, the whole point of that scene is to illustrate that politicians like or the people in charge like to sit there and verbally pat themselves on the back in their efforts while completely missing the point.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Matt Weth
utterances.text: Dickensian indeed, and still no progress.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Matt Weth
utterances.text: Yeah, Dickensian, rooms without windows and ceilings.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Matt Weth
utterances.text: Do you know what the sound environment is like in a tin box like that?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Matt Weth
utterances.text: You can hear everything within a 50-foot radius.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Matt Weth
utterances.text: It echoes.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Matt Weth
utterances.text: The specific issue that I had during my time there, I did not have one night of decent sleep in that facility.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Matt Weth
utterances.text: Six months straight of sleep deprivation.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Matt Weth
utterances.text: That's beyond inhumane.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Matt Weth
utterances.text: That's abusive.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Matt Weth
utterances.text: There's a lawsuit forthcoming because I have receipts.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Matt Weth
utterances.text: I contacted Julie Wan's office.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Matt Weth
utterances.text: I took a picture of the rules that I signed off.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Matt Weth
utterances.text: I have receipts on all this, by the way.

chapters.summary: Morano apologizes for Weth's experience and asks what should be first on the agenda; Weth recommends a paid veteran on staff who has been through the system, criticizes grandstanding, and Morano offers to stay in touch.
chapters.title: Morano asks Weth for first agenda item

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: Mr.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: Weth, one, I'm very sorry for your experience.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: I don't accept your apology.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: I appreciate the sentiments.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: Two, I appreciate your service very much.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: Thank you for your service in the Air Force.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: If you're sitting where we're sitting, I think everybody here really wants to improve conditions.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: What's the first item that should be on our agenda?

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: What should we do?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Matt Weth
utterances.text: This is the suggestion that I had.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Matt Weth
utterances.text: I had a good answer for that.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Matt Weth
utterances.text: And I'm almost loathe to give it now after having shown up and witnessed these proceedings.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Matt Weth
utterances.text: I'll still give the recommendation, but I don't think I'll attach my name to it or volunteer or volunteer myself.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Matt Weth
utterances.text: You need a veteran paid on staff who has been through this, who knows the issue from both sides, who can report not only to you.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Matt Weth
utterances.text: But to the public who can make the public aware of this whole issue.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Matt Weth
utterances.text: Not only all the malfeasance and deterioration that's going on, but hey, it's an opportunity for good PR for you guys too, right?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Matt Weth
utterances.text: Yeah, yeah, yeah.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: West.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Matt Weth
utterances.text: Yeah, yeah.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Matt Weth
utterances.text: You're very welcome.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Matt Weth
utterances.text: I'd volunteer for that position.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Matt Weth
utterances.text: But again, my qualifier, like, okay, how's this?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Matt Weth
utterances.text: Councilperson Marano, earlier at some point, you said you've been accused of grandstanding before.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Matt Weth
utterances.text: Oh, really?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Matt Weth
utterances.text: What?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Matt Weth
utterances.text: After I had to sit through a half an hour of thank yous and hellos and congratulations so everyone could hear their name?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Matt Weth
utterances.text: Boy.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Matt Weth
utterances.text: We live on grandstanding around here, huh?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Matt Weth
utterances.text: That would...

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Matt Weth
utterances.text: Never fly in the military.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Matt Weth
utterances.text: We don't have a half an hour for that.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: Mr.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: Weth, I hope we can stay in touch.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: I understand it's politics.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: No, I hope we can stay in touch.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: I do want to get to these other panels.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: Oh, okay.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: I see what's going on here.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Matt Weth
utterances.text: Pardon?

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: I'll give you my number and my email, and we'll stay in touch.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Matt Weth
utterances.text: Am I getting cut off here?

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: Well, yeah.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Matt Weth
utterances.text: Is this the gaffe?

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: We're giving everybody five minutes.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Matt Weth
utterances.text: Oh, that was five minutes already?

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: It was about 10 minutes, but we are giving everybody five minutes to try to accommodate as many people as possible.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Matt Weth
utterances.text: It took a couple hours waiting to get that.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Matt Weth
utterances.text: I appreciate it.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Matt Weth
utterances.text: And I don't want to take over anyone else's time.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: Which is why we've been very flexible with the time.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: Thank you, sir, and thank you for your service.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: Thank you, gentlemen, for your perspective and for your testimony.

chapters.summary: Morano calls Kristen Miller, Graham Horn, Coco Culhane, and Derek Coy, and jokes about spoilers.
chapters.title: Morano calls provider panel

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: At this point, we will call up the next panel.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: This is a panel of providers.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: Let me welcome Kristen Miller, Graham Horn, Coco Colhaney, and Derek Coy.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: And I would just ask, irrespective of what you talk about, I actually am one of the few people that still haven't seen The Wire.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: So if you're going to give away any plot points from any of the seasons of television shows, I would just appreciate it if you would say spoiler alert before doing so, irrespective of the show, even if it's a show you assume everybody has seen.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: So why don't we go, we'll go left to right.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: We'll begin with you.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: Please identify yourself and get started.

chapters.summary: Horn introduces himself from NYLAG, supports Intro 897, opposes forced removals, describes shelter accessibility issues, curfews, policing, and the need for compassion.
chapters.title: Graham Horn testifies on Intro 897 and shelter conditions

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Graham Horn
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Graham Horn
utterances.text: Thank you for holding this hearing.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: Just turn your mic on and make sure it's nice and close.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: It is on, but I'll bring it closer.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: Great, thank you.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Graham Horn
utterances.text: My name is Graham Horn.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Graham Horn
utterances.text: I'm a coordinating attorney on NILAG's Shelter and Economic Stability Project.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Graham Horn
utterances.text: NILAG also boasts a robust veterans practice.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Graham Horn
utterances.text: Also within our public benefits unit, I would like to personally thank all former and active service members.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Graham Horn
utterances.text: And I would also like to thank the city administration and commissioners for staying to listen.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Graham Horn
utterances.text: That's an incredibly welcome change.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Graham Horn
utterances.text: We are supportive of Intro 897, which does not include language encouraging forced removals.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Graham Horn
utterances.text: But instead calls for continued efforts to offer shelter and warming bus options during cold and severe weather.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Graham Horn
utterances.text: Forced removals to shelter are violent disruptions that have absolutely no productive consequences.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Graham Horn
utterances.text: People do not choose to sleep outside.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Graham Horn
utterances.text: Rather, congregate shelter does not meet the needs of its intended residents.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Graham Horn
utterances.text: My written testimony describes many fixes to shelter that would work towards the goal of limiting street homelessness, not through force, but by offering a stabilizing and supportive alternative.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Graham Horn
utterances.text: would be to restore trust between street outreach workers and our unhoused neighbors, and also to expand the availability of single and double room placements within our shelters.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Graham Horn
utterances.text: Additionally, our buildings suffer from enormous structural accessibility issues.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Graham Horn
utterances.text: Even our new mail intake facility is inaccessible.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Graham Horn
utterances.text: The difficulty of obtaining reasonable accommodations without an advocate's additional support.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Graham Horn
utterances.text: Unavailability of shelter transfers even after violent events.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Graham Horn
utterances.text: Curfew policies, intake onerousness, intense policing, difficulty of bringing emotional support animals even when credentialed into the spaces.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Graham Horn
utterances.text: If our goal is to reduce unsheltered homelessness, we must work through compassion to meet the needs of those who currently cannot accept placement in our shelters.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Graham Horn
utterances.text: On our coldest nights, we must offer warmth.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Graham Horn
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: Thank you.

chapters.summary: Culhane says the city should have known the grant terms, suggests trans veterans are being used as cover, asks about performance and a sexual assault report, and says veterans choose the street due to addiction and safety concerns.
chapters.title: Coco Culhane questions GPD contract and safety at Borden

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Coco Culhane
utterances.text: Hi, I'm Coco Colhane from the Veteran Advocacy Project, and we provide free legal services to veterans, focusing on those with mental health conditions.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Coco Culhane
utterances.text: I want to just start where this all kind of seems to have started with the contract.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Coco Culhane
utterances.text: You know, the city should have known anyway, if they didn't, that...

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Coco Culhane
utterances.text: These conditions were a part of it.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Coco Culhane
utterances.text: They were published in January 2026 as the terms and conditions on page two.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Coco Culhane
utterances.text: So it seems that trans vets are being used as cover.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Coco Culhane
utterances.text: And so, you know, would just hope that the city would answer to that, why they applied if they, you know, if those conditions are already there.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Coco Culhane
utterances.text: And they're involved in litigation, I believe, in other areas with federal policy.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Coco Culhane
utterances.text: So it would be hard to believe that they weren't aware of it.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Coco Culhane
utterances.text: And the other thing is I'm just wondering why we're not asking more about the performance side and why, you know, what happened.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Coco Culhane
utterances.text: And I understand there are limitations.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Coco Culhane
utterances.text: It's a federal agency, it's a contract, but I hope that these questions remain.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Coco Culhane
utterances.text: So part of my organization started out wandering the halls of the VA and Borden Avenue.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Coco Culhane
utterances.text: And over the years, we've had 518 veterans who have called Borden home for a short while.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Coco Culhane
utterances.text: But I can't tell you the number of other veterans who have said, I'm choosing the street instead.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Coco Culhane
utterances.text: And for two main reasons.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Coco Culhane
utterances.text: One, addiction issues.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Coco Culhane
utterances.text: that the reports are that it's very hard to stay sober.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Coco Culhane
utterances.text: There's availability of drugs is difficult.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Coco Culhane
utterances.text: And then safety.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Coco Culhane
utterances.text: And this is another thing I'm wondering why we're not talking about.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Coco Culhane
utterances.text: There were, you know, in several of the news reports, this

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Coco Culhane
utterances.text: report about a sexual assault.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Coco Culhane
utterances.text: I've heard that it was, you know, an ICL employee.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Coco Culhane
utterances.text: Like, why is that not being pursued today?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Coco Culhane
utterances.text: And I'm not saying it happened or not.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Coco Culhane
utterances.text: I have no idea, but it seems concerning enough that it should be a focus.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Coco Culhane
utterances.text: You know, the conditions are really important.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Coco Culhane
utterances.text: The roof, you know, we've known about a leaking roof for years.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Coco Culhane
utterances.text: And so that's really shameful.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Coco Culhane
utterances.text: But equally as important, if not more, should be safety.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Coco Culhane
utterances.text: And it's just strange that it hasn't been asked about.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Coco Culhane
utterances.text: And so we would just hope that these things are followed up on because we can have these hearings, we can have the press conferences, but if there's no follow-up, it doesn't matter, and we're back here in a couple of years.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Coco Culhane
utterances.text: Thank you.

chapters.summary: Morano asks if the city knew of federal conditions before applying; Culhane says one would think so but she does not know for a fact; Morano asks if Borden has improved, and Culhane says she has not visited recently and the council should listen to veterans.
chapters.title: Morano asks Culhane about grant chronology and improvements

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: A couple of quick questions, Ms.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: Colhaney.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: One, thank you for everything your group does.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: I appreciate it.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: Just to clarify what you said about the federal grant.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: So the city, just so everybody understands the chronology, the city was aware of the federal government's policy when it comes to

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: gender and transgender veterans, and then they still applied for the grant knowing of those conditions?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Coco Culhane
utterances.text: I don't, sorry, let me be very clear.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Coco Culhane
utterances.text: I don't know that.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Coco Culhane
utterances.text: I'm saying.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Coco Culhane
utterances.text: that one would think they did because they were published in January and the application went in, from my understanding, in February.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Coco Culhane
utterances.text: So, and they're part of a lot of other conditions that have, you know, in the last two years developed, creating a lot of challenges for providers and social services.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Coco Culhane
utterances.text: And again, my understanding is the city is involved in these things and knows

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Coco Culhane
utterances.text: So one would think that when they applied, they did.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Coco Culhane
utterances.text: I don't know that for a fact.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: Because you've been following the situation at Borden Avenue for a long time, you've heard a lot of the criticisms and complaints over the years.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: And the last hearing on veterans'homelessness, I'm betting you're familiar with, you probably were even here.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: Have you seen improvements at the Borden Avenue situation based on what you've heard today, whether it's data or whether it's anecdotal?

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: Do you see things moving in the right direction from your perspective?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Coco Culhane
utterances.text: I have not been there myself personally in the last several years, so I don't feel I'm...
